'''Aeneas Demetrius Williams''' ({{IPAc-en|ə|ˈ|n|iː|ə|s}} {{respell|un|NEE|us}}; born January 29, 1968) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] and [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for 14 seasons. He played [[college football]] for the [[Southern Jaguars football|Southern Jaguars]] and was selected in the third round of the [[1991 NFL draft]] by the [[Phoenix Cardinals]], where he spent 10 seasons. During his final four seasons, he was a member of the [[St. Louis Rams]]. Williams received eight [[Pro Bowl]] selections and three first-team [[All-Pro]] honors, as well as being on the second [[National Football League 1990s All-Decade Team|NFL 1990s All-Decade Team]]. He was inducted into the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] in 2014.

==Early life==
Williams was born in [[New Orleans, Louisiana]], to Lawrence and Lillian Williams. Aeneas is the youngest of 3 brothers, Malcolm and Achilles.<ref name="auto">{{Cite web |last=Williams |first=Darrell |date=August 19, 2014 |title=Aeneas Williams showed early promise at Fortier High School |url=https://www.nola.com/sports/high_schools/article_27fd6de0-4b95-5262-b569-7a9bc9ccb89b.html |access-date=September 25, 2023 |website=NOLA.com}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web |last=Harris |first=Terrance |date=July 29, 2014 |title=2014 Pro Football Hall of Fame: Aeneas Williams' ascension to greatness began at early age in New Orleans |url=https://www.nola.com/sports/article_5b16b579-6b0e-5640-9a5b-c6d6151d9b84.html |access-date=September 25, 2023 |website=NOLA.com}}</ref> He attended the now defunct [[Alcee Fortier High School]], where he played football on a team with three future [[National Football League|NFL]] players: [[Maurice Hurst (cornerback)|Maurice Hurst]], [[Kevin Lewis (defensive back)|Kevin Lewis]], and [[Ashley Ambrose]]. In 1985, the Fortier Tarpons went undefeated through 10 games and won the District 10-4A championship and proceeded to the Class 4A semifinals.<ref name="auto" /> Aeneas was selected to the all-district team as a strong safety that season.<ref name="auto" />

==College career==
Williams was not offered a scholarship when he graduated high school.  He attended [[Southern University]], the same school his brother Achilles attended, planning to simply get his accounting degree. "Our parents always expected that we would go to college and get our degree," he explained.  "(Playing football) never crossed by mind, I was preparing for the rest of my life."<ref>{{Cite web |last=East |first=Les |date=August 15, 2014 |title=Aeneas Williams found himself at Southern |url=https://www.theadvocate.com/baton_rouge/article_0a072679-207c-56f4-b15e-62874f82b79b.html |access-date=September 25, 2023 |website=The Advocate}}</ref>

At Southern, he concentrated on his academics, not playing football until his junior year.  Eventually, after being encouraged by his old high school teammate [[Maurice Hurst (cornerback)|Maurice Hurst]], he decided to join the team as a walk-on.  He started out playing mostly on special teams, but made the starting lineup in the 5th game.  Williams kept his involvement with the football team a secret from his family until he made the travel squad for the 2nd game of the season. In the following season, Williams was named to the All-Southwestern Athletic Conference team after leading the conference with seven interceptions.  In 1990, Williams stayed on the team as a [[graduate student]] and fifth year senior in order to improve his draft status.  He made the All-SWAC team again and tied the [[NCAA Division I-AA|Division I-AA]] record for most interceptions with eleven.

Williams finished his college career with 20 interceptions and 28 pass deflections.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Aeneas Williams – Hall of Fame |url=https://allstatesugarbowl.org/classic/aeneas-williams-hall-of-fame/ |access-date=August 10, 2021 |archive-date=August 10, 2021 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20210810225655/https://allstatesugarbowl.org/classic/aeneas-williams-hall-of-fame/ |url-status=dead }}</ref>

===Phoenix/Arizona Cardinals===
====1991====
The [[Phoenix Cardinals]] selected Williams in the third round (59th overall) of the [[1991 NFL draft]]. He was the sixth cornerback selected. He became [[List of Southern Jaguars in the NFL draft|Southern's ninth highest player selected in the history of the NFL Draft]] and their 55th player selected in the draft since [[1967 NFL/AFL draft|1967]].

On July 19, 1991, the Cardinals signed Williams to a three–year, $960,000 rookie contract that included a [[signing bonus]] of $200,000.<ref name="spotrac">{{cite web| title=Spotrac.com: Aeneas Williams contracts|url=https://www.spotrac.com/nfl/player/_/id/13930/aeneas-williams |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=Spotrac.com}}</ref> Throughout training camp, Williams competed against [[Cedric Mack]], [[Robert Massey]], and [[Jay Taylor (defensive back)|Jay Taylor]] to be the No. 1 starting cornerback under new defensive coordinator [[Fritz Shurmur]].<ref>{{cite web|title=NFL Camps |url=https://www.oklahoman.com/story/news/1991/08/16/nfl-camps/62519811007/ |access-date=July 9, 2025| newspaper=Oklahoman|date=August 16, 1991}}</ref><ref name="size"/><ref>{{cite web| title=47 days until Week 1: Remembering No. 47 Cedric Mack| url=https://cardswire.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/cardinals/2018/07/24/47-days-until-week-1-remembering-no-47-cedric-mack/79850539007/ |access-date=July 9, 2025 |website=cardswire.usatoday.com| date=July 24, 2018|last=Root| first=Jess|language=en}}</ref> On August 23, 1991, the Phoenix Cardinals unexpectedly cut Cedric Mack as part of their final roster cuts.<ref>{{cite web| title=Chargers' roster down to 47-men: Football; Bayless, McEwen among those cut, but might be back
|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1991-08-27-sp-1527-story.html |access-date=July 9, 2025| newspaper=LA Times|date=August 27, 1991}}</ref> Head coach [[Joe Bugel]] named Williams and Robert Massey as the starting cornerbacks to begin the season.<ref name="size">{{cite web| title=Another in a series of NFL preseason sizeups: the Phoenix Cardinals
|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1991/08/23/Another-in-a-series-of-NFL-preseason-sizeups-the-Phoenix-Cardinals/3243682920000/ |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=UPI.com|date=August 23, 1991}}</ref>

On September 1, 1991, Williams made his professional regular season debut and earned his first career start in the [[1991 Phoenix Cardinals season|Phoenix Cardinals']] season-opener at the [[1991 Los Angeles Rams season|Los Angeles Rams]] and recorded three solo tackles and had his first career interception on a pass thrown by [[Jim Everett]] as they won 24–14.<ref>{{cite web| title=Phoenix Cardinals at Los Angeles Rams — September 1st, 1991|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199109010ram.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref><ref name="NFL91"/> The following week, he recorded three solo tackles, set a season-high with two fumble recoveries, and intercepted a pass running back [[Keith Byars]] attempted to throw as he was hit by linebacker [[Garth Jax]] during a 26–10 win at the [[1991 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] in Week 2.<ref>{{cite web| title=Phoenix Cardinals at Philadelphia Eagles — September 8th, 1991|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199109080phi.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=When West Meets East| url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1991/09/16/when-west-meets-east-with-a-win-in-philly-phoenix-showed-its-an-nfc-east-team-in-every-way-except-geographically |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=vault.si.com| date=September 16, 1991|last=King|first=Peter}}</ref> In Week 12, he set a season-high with nine combined tackles (eight solo) during a 10–14 loss at the [[1991 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]].<ref name="NFL91">{{cite web|title=NFL.com: Aeneas Williams stats; Game Logs (1991)|
url=https://www.nfl.com/players/aeneas-williams/stats/logs/1991/-except-geographically |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=NFL.com}}</ref> The following week, Williams recorded four solo tackles, set a season-high with three pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by [[Jim McMahon]] as the Cardinals lost 34–14 to the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 13.<ref>{{cite web| title=Philadelphia Eagles at Phoenix Cardinals — November 24th, 1991|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199111240crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref><ref name="NFL91"/> On December 15, 1991, Williams made four solo tackles, two pass deflections, and set a season-high with two interceptions on passes thrown by [[John Elway]] during a 19–24 loss at the [[1991 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Phoenix Cardinals at Denver Broncos — December 15th, 1991|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199112150den.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref><ref name="NFL91"/> He finished his rookie season with 66 combined tackles (58 solo), 10 pass deflections, six interceptions, and two fumble recoveries in 16 games and 15 starts.<ref name="NFL91"/><ref name="career">{{cite web|title=Pro-Football-Reference: Aeneas Williams Career Overview|
url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WillAe00.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref> His six interceptions tied for the most in the NFC in 1991, alongside [[Deion Sanders]], [[Tim McKyer]], and [[Ray Crockett]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1991 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1991/draft.htm |access-date=May 7, 2023 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

====1992====
He returned to training camp slated as the No. 1 starting cornerback with Robert Massey and Lorenzo Lynch competing for the other starting role.<ref>{{cite web| title=Dizziness Keeps Willis Out| url=https://www.chicagotribune.com/1992/08/16/dizziness-keeps-willis-out/ |access-date=July 10, 2025| newspaper=Chicago Tribune| date=August 16, 1992}}</ref> Head coach Joe Bugel named Williams and Lorenzo Lynch the starting cornerbacks to begin the season.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Former Bethel Players Keep Plugging Away |url=https://www.dailypress.com/1992/08/21/former-bethel-player-keeps-plugging-away/ |access-date=July 10, 2025 |website=DailyPress.com| date=August 21, 1992|language=en}}</ref> Prior to Week 4, defensive coordinator Fritz Shurmur demoted [[Lorenzo Lynch]] to a backup and replaced him in the starting lineup with [[Robert Massey]] for the rest of the season.<ref name="nomassey">{{cite web| title=Around the NFL: No Massey| url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1993/10/13/around-the-nfl/b70cf7fe-5600-4c75-b355-c49e498d7d75/ |access-date=July 10, 2025| newspaper=Washington Post| date=October 13, 1993}}</ref> On November 22, 1992, Williams set a season-high with seven combined tackles (six solo), made one pass deflection, and intercepted a pass attempt by [[Troy Aikman]] during a 16–10 loss against the [[1992 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Dallas Cowboys at Phoenix Cardinals — November 22nd, 1992|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199211220crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> He started all 16 games throughout the [[1992 NFL season]] for the first time in his career and made 50 combined tackles (39 solo), 10 pass deflections, and three interceptions.<ref name="NFL92">{{cite web|title=NFL.com: Aeneas Williams stats; Game Logs (1992)|
url=https://www.nfl.com/players/aeneas-williams/stats/logs/1992/ |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=NFL.com}}</ref>

====1993====
He returned to training camp slated as the ''de facto'' No. 1 starting cornerback. [[Robert Massey]] was a contract holdout and would miss the entire preseason as well as the first seven games of the season.<ref name="nomassey"/> Head coach [[Joe Bugel]] named Williams and Lorenzo Lynch as the starting cornerbacks to begin the season.

On September 5, 1993, Williams started in the [[1993 Phoenix Cardinals season|Phoenix Cardinals']] season-opener at the [[1993 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] and set a season-high with six solo tackles and made one pass deflection as they lost 17–23.<ref name="NFL93">{{cite web|title=NFL.com: Aeneas Williams stats; Game Logs (1993)|
url=https://www.nfl.com/players/aeneas-williams/stats/logs/1992/ |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=NFL.com}}</ref> On October 31, 1993, Williams made six combined tackles (five solo), one pass deflection, and scored a career-high two touchdowns on an interception return and a return on a fumble recovery during a 20–17 loss against the [[1993 New Orleans Saints season|New Orleans Saints]].<ref>{{cite web| title=New Orleans Saints at Phoenix Cardinals — October 31st, 1993|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199310310crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> He scored the first touchdown of his career in the first quarter after recovering a fumble by wide receiver [[Quinn Early]] and returning it 20–yards for a touchdown.<ref name="UPI"/> The first pick-six of his career occurred in the second quarter after he intercepted a pass [[Wade Wilson (American football)|Wade Wilson]] threw to wide receiver [[Eric Martin (wide receiver)|Eric Martin]] and returned it 46–yards for a touchdown.<ref name="UPI">{{cite web| title=Saints 20, Cardinals 17
|url=https://www.upi.com/Archives/1993/10/31/Saints-20-Cardinals-17/2303752040000/ |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=UPI.com|date=October 31, 1993}}</ref> The following game, Williams recorded three combined tackles (two solo), set a season-high with two pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by [[Ken O'Brien]] as the Cardinals defeated the [[1993 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] 3–16 in Week 10.<ref>{{cite web| title=Philadelphia Eagles at Phoenix Cardinals — November 7th, 1993|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199311070crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> He started all 16 games throughout the [[1993 NFL season]] and made 47 combined tackles (43 solo), 12 pass deflections, two interceptions, two touchdowns, and one fumble recovery.<ref name="career"/><ref name="NFL93"/> He was selected to play in the [[1994 Pro Bowl]] to mark the first [[Pro Bowl]] selection of his career.

====1994====
On January 24, 1994, the Arizona Cardinals fired head coach [[Joe Bugel]] after they ended the [[1993 NFL season]] with a 7–9 record.<ref>{{cite web| title=Cardinals Dismiss Bugel After Four Years| url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/archive/sports/1994/01/25/cardinals-dismiss-bugel-after-four-years-eye-cowboys-turner/a149877e-6456-45ff-80d2-01a68231bf85/ |access-date=July 9, 2025 |newspaper=Washington Post| date=January 25, 1994| last=Litsky| first=Frank|language=en}}</ref> On February 3, 1994, the Cardinals hired former [[1992 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles']] head coach [[Buddy Ryan]] to takeover as their new head coach.<ref>{{cite web| title=PRO FOOTBALL: CARDINALS ADD SOME PUNCH WITH HIRING OF RYAN| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1994/02/04/sports/pro-football-cardinals-add-some-punch-with-hiring-of-ryan.html |access-date=July 9, 2025 |newspaper=New York Times| date=February 4, 1994|language=en}}</ref> On February 17, 1994, the [[1994 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] signed Williams to a two–year, $3 million contract extension that included a signing bonus of $900,000.<ref name="spotrac"/><ref name="sfgate">{{cite web| title=Hostetler Stakes Down To 2 Teams?| url=https://www.sfgate.com/sports/article/Hostetler-Stakes-Down-To-2-Teams-2992340.php |access-date=July 9, 2025 |website=sfgate.com| date=February 17, 1994|language=en}}</ref><ref>{{cite web| title=PRO FOOTBALL: NOTEBOOK; Beat the Cap Turns Into an Expensive New Game for Owners| url=https://www.nytimes.com/1993/12/26/sports/pro-football-notebook-beat-the-cap-turns-into-an-expensive-new-game-for-owners.html |access-date=July 9, 2025 |newspaper=New York Times| date=February 19, 1994| last=Litsky| first=Frank|language=en}}</ref> 

Entering training camp, Williams remained as the No. 1 starting cornerback under the new defensive coordinator [[Ronnie Jones (American football)|Ronnie Jones]]. Head coach Buddy Ryan named Williams and [[James Williams (cornerback)|James Williams]] the starting cornerbacks to begin the season.<ref>{{cite web| title=Fans in Arizona| url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1994-09-02-sp-34005-story.html |access-date=July 9, 2025 |newspaper=LA Times| date=September 2, 1994|language=en}}</ref> 

On September 18, 1994, Williams made five solo tackles, one pass break-up, and had his first interception of the season on a pass [[Vinny Testaverde]] threw to wide receiver [[Mark Carrier (wide receiver)|Mark Carrier]] during a 0–32 loss at the [[1994 Cleveland Browns season|Cleveland Browns]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Phoenix Cardinals at Cleveland Browns — September 18th, 1994|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199409180cle.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> On October 16, 1994, Williams made two solo tackles, two pass deflections, and set a season-high with two interceptions on pass attempts thrown by [[Heath Shuler]] during a 19–16 overtime victory at the [[1994 Washington Redskins season|Washington Redskins]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Phoenix Cardinals at Washington Redskins — October 16th, 1994|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199410160was.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> In Week 12, he recorded two solo tackles, set a season-high with three pass deflections, and intercepted a pass [[Randall Cunningham]] threw to wide receiver [[Fred Barnett]] as the Cardinals defeated the [[1994 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] 6–12.<ref>{{cite web| title=Philadelphia Eagles at Phoenix Cardinals — November 20th, 1994 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199411200crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> On December 11, 1994, Williams made five solo tackles, one pass deflection, and made his ninth interception of the season on a pass thrown by [[Heath Shuler]] to wide receiver [[Olanda Truitt]] as the Cardinals defeated the Washington Redskins 15–17.<ref>{{cite web| title=Washington Redskins at Phoenix Cardinals — December 11th, 1994 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199412110crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> He started all 16 games for the third consecutive season and made 42 combined tackles (40 solo).
He set a new career-high in interceptions (9) and passes defended (26).<ref>{{Cite web |title=1994 NFL Defense |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1994/defense.htm |access-date=2025-04-12 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>
====1995====
Head coach Buddy Ryan named Williams the No. 1 starting cornerback to begin the season, but paired him with [[Patrick Hunter]] following the departure of James Williams. On October 15, 1995, Williams recorded three solo tackles, set a season-high with four pass deflections, and returned an interception by [[Gus Frerotte]] to wide receiver [[Michael Westbrook]] for a 28–yard touchdown as the Cardinals defeated the [[1995 Washington Redskins season|Washington Redskins]] 20–24.<ref>{{cite web| title=Washington Redskins at Arizona Cardinals — October 15th, 1995|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199510150crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> On December 9, 1995, Williams made six solo tackles, two pass deflections, and set a season-high with two interceptions on passes thrown by [[Stan Humphries]] during a 25–28 loss at the [[1995 San Diego Chargers season|San Diego Chargers]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Arizona Cardinals at San Diego Chargers — December 9th, 1995|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199512090sdg.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref>  In Week 17, he set a season-high with nine combined tackles (six solo), had one pass break-up, and intercepted a pass attempt thrown by Troy Aikman to wide receiver [[Michael Irvin]] and returned it 48–yards for a touchdown during a 37–13 loss against the [[1995 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]]. On December 27, 1995, the [[1995 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] announced their decision to fire head coach [[Buddy Ryan]] after they finished the [[1995 NFL season]] with a 4–12 record.<ref>{{cite web| title=Buddy Ryan loses job in Phoenix Cardinals oust| url=https://www.spokesman.com/stories/1995/dec/27/buddy-ryan-loses-job-in-phoenix-cardinals-oust/ |access-date=July 9, 2025 |website=spokesman.com| date=December 27, 1995|language=en}}</ref> He started all 16 games and made 62 combined tackles (52 solo), 22 pass deflections, six interceptions, three fumble recoveries, and scored two touchdowns.<ref name="career"/><ref name="NFL95">{{cite web|title=NFL.com: Aeneas Williams stats; Game Logs (1995)|
url=https://www.nfl.com/players/aeneas-williams/stats/logs/1995/ |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=NFL.com}}</ref>

====1996====
On February 26, 1996, the [[1996 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] re-signed Williams to a six–year, $17 million contract extension that included a signing bonus of $6 million.<ref>{{cite web| title=CARDS RE-SIGN CORNER; COWBOYS LOSE STARTER| url=https://www.deseret.com/1996/2/27/19227382/cards-re-sign-corner-cowboys-lose-starter/ |access-date=July 9, 2025 |website=deseret.com| date=February 27, 1996|language=en}}</ref><ref name="spotrac"/><ref name="sfgate"/> The Cardinals had hired [[Vince Tobin]] earlier in the month to be the new head coach.<ref>{{cite web| title=Cardinals name Vince Tobin head coach|
url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-1996-02-08-sp-33673-story.html |access-date=July 9, 2025 |website=[[Los Angeles Times]]| date=February 6, 1996|language=en}}</ref> Following the departures of [[Lorenzo Lynch]] and [[Patrick Hunter]], Williams was projected to begin the season alongside [[Tito Paul]].<ref>{{cite web|title=5 Arizona Cardinals|url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1996/08/01/5-arizona-cardinals |access-date=July 10, 2025| website=Vault.SI.com| date=August 1, 1996| last=Zimmerman| first=Paul}}</ref> On August 27, 1996, the Cardinals claimed cornerback [[Ronnie Bradford]] off waivers after he was cut by the [[1996 Denver Broncos season|Denver Broncos]]. Head coach Vince Tobin named Williams the No. 1 starting cornerback to begin the season and chose to start safety [[Brent Alexander]] alongside him as the No. 2 starting cornerback for the first two games. Defensive coordinator [[Dave McGinnis]] elected to promote Ronnie Bradford to the No. 2 starting cornerback beginning in Week 3.

On October 27, 1996, Williams made seven combined tackles (six solo), two pass deflections, and set a season-high with two interceptions thrown by [[Frank Reich]] as the Cardinals lost 31–21 against the [[1996 New York Jets season|New York Jets]] to give them their first win of the season after eight consecutive losses.<ref>{{cite web| title=New York Jets at Arizona Cardinals — October 27th, 1996 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199610270crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> On November 17, 1996, Williams made eight combined tackles (six solo), two pass deflections, and intercepted a pass by [[Dave Brown (quarterback)|Dave Brown]] as the Cardinals defeated the [[1996 New York Giants season|New York Giants]] 23–31.<ref>{{cite web| title=New York Giants at Arizona Cardinals — November 17th, 1996 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199611170crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> The following week, he recorded seven combined tackles (five solo), two pass deflections, one interception, and had his first career sack on [[Ty Detmer]] for a six–yard loss during a 30–36 victory against the [[1996 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] in Week 13.<ref>{{cite web| title=Philadelphia Eagles at Arizona Cardinals — November 24th, 1996 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199611240crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> In Week 15, he set a season-high with nine solo tackles and had two pass break-ups during a 6–10 loss to the [[1996 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]]. On December 22, 1996, Williams made two solo tackles, one pass deflection, and had a pick-six on an interception he returned for a 65–yard touchdown that was thrown by Ty Detmer during a 19–29 loss at the Philadelphia Eagles.<ref>{{cite web| title=Arizona Cardinals at Philadelphia Eagles — December 22nd, 1996 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199612220phi.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> He started all 16 games for the fifth consecutive season and set a career-high with 77 combined tackles (65 solo) while also recording 18 pass deflections, six interceptions, one sack, and one touchdown.<ref name="career"/>

====1997====
The [[1997 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] selected cornerbacks [[Tom Knight (American football)|Tom Knight]] in the first-round (9th overall) and [[Ty Howard]] in the third-round (84th overall) of the [[1997 NFL draft]] following the departure of Ronnie Bradford.<ref>{{cite web|title=4 Arizona Cardinals|url=https://vault.si.com/vault/1997/07/16/4-arizona-cardinals |access-date=July 10, 2025| website=Vault.SI.com| date=July 16, 1997| last=Zimmerman| first=Paul}}</ref> Head coach [[Vince Tobin]] named Williams the No. 1 starting cornerback to begin the season and paired him with rookie Tom Knight.<ref>{{cite web|title=SCOUTING REPORT: CARDINALS AT BUCS // KEY MATCHUPS| url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1997/09/28/scouting-report-cardinals-at-bucs-key-matchups/ |access-date=July 10, 2025| website=TampaBay.com| date=September 28, 1997| last=Stroud| first=Rick}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=Sharpe cashes in with $7.2-million deal| url=https://www.tampabay.com/archive/1997/07/17/sharpe-cashes-in-with-7-2-million-deal/ |access-date=July 10, 2025| website=TampaBay.com| date=July 17, 1997| last=Stroud| first=Rick}}</ref>

On September 28, 1997, Williams recorded five solo tackles, set a season-high with three pass deflections, and returned an interception by [[Trent Dilfer]] 42–yards for a touchdown during an 18–19 loss at the [[1997 Tampa Bay Buccaneers season|Tampa Bay Buccaneers]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Arizona Cardinals at Tampa Bay Buccaneers — September 28th, 1997 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199709280tam.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> In Week 7, Williams made six combined tackles (five solo), two pass deflections, and had his second pick-six of the season after intercepting a pass by [[Danny Kanell]] to wide receiver [[Amani Toomer]] during a 27–13 loss against the [[1997 New York Giants season|New York Giants]].<ref>{{cite web| title=New York Giants at Arizona Cardinals — October 12th, 1997 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199710120crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> The following week, he set a season-high with seven combined tackles (four solo) and made one pass deflection during a 10–13 overtime loss at the [[1997 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] in Week 8.<ref name="NFL97">{{cite web|title=NFL.com: Aeneas Williams stats; Game Logs (1997)|
url=https://www.nfl.com/players/aeneas-williams/stats/logs/1997/ |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=NFL.com}}</ref> In Week 16, he made two solo tackles, a pass deflection, and had his sixth interception of the season on a pass by [[Billy Joe Hobert]] to wide receiver [[Andre Hastings]] during a 10–24 loss at the [[1997 New Orleans Saints season|New Orleans Saints]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Arizona Cardinals at New Orleans Saints — December 14th, 1997 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199712140nor.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> He started all 16 games and recorded 62 combined tackles (48 solo), 18 pass deflections, six interceptions, two touchdowns, and a forced fumble.<ref name="career"/>

====1998====
The Cardinals selected cornerback [[Corey Chavous]] in the second-round (33rd overall) of the [[1998 NFL draft]]. Head coach [[Vince Tobin]] named Williams and Tom Knight the starting cornerbacks to begin the season. On September 6, 1998, Williams started in the Cardinals' season-opener at the [[1998 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]] and set a season-high with 11 combined tackles (10 solo) as they lost 10–38. In Week 4, Tom Knight suffered a hamstring injury and remained inactive for the next four games (Weeks 5–9) and was replaced by [[J. B. Brown (cornerback)|J. B. Brown]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Week 13 Injury Report |url=https://www.jt-sw.com/football/pro/index.nsf/Documents/1998-ir-13 |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=jt-sw.com| date=November 13, 1998}}</ref> In Week 6, Williams made one tackle, a pass deflection, and had his lone interception of the season on a pass [[Erik Kramer]] threw to wide receiver [[Curtis Conway]] as the Cardinals defeated the [[1998 Chicago Bears season|Chicago Bears]] 7–20.<ref>{{cite web| title=Chicago Bears at Arizona Cardinals — October 11th, 1998 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199810110crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> Defensive coordinator [[Dave McGinnis]] named Corey Chavous the No. 2 starting cornerback for the last five games of the season.<ref>{{cite web|title=Breaking down the Cardinals vs. Vikings
|url=https://static.espn.go.com/nfl/playoffs98/news/1999/990106/01030954.html |access-date=July 10, 2025| website=static.espn.go.com| date=January 6, 1999}}</ref><ref>{{cite web|title=EAGLES HAVE A HISTORY VS. CARDS * THE SERIES IS TIED, WHICH BOTH AGREE TO, BUT THEY ARE AT ODDS AS TO HOW MANY GAMES WERE PLAYED.
|url=https://www.mcall.com/1998/12/13/eagles-have-a-history-vs-cards-the-series-is-tied-which-both-agree-to-but-they-are-at-odds-as-to-how-many-games-were-played/ |access-date=July 10, 2025| website=mcall.com| date=December 13, 1998}}</ref> He started all 16 games for the seventh consecutive season and recorded 70 combined tackles (52 solo), seven pass deflections, one sack, and made one interception.<ref name="career"/>

The [[1998 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] finished the [[1998 NFL season]] with a 9–7 record, marking the only time they had a winning record during Williams' entire 10–seasons. On January 2, 1999, Williams started in the first playoff game of his career and recorded two solo tackles and had a game–high two interceptions on passes thrown by [[Troy Aikman]] during a 20–7 victory at the [[1998 Dallas Cowboys season|Dallas Cowboys]] in the NFC Wild-Card Game.<ref>{{cite web| title=Wild-Card — Arizona Cardinals at Dallas Cowboys — January 2nd, 1999 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199901020dal.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> On January 10, 1999, Williams started in the Divisional Round at the [[1998 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota Vikings]] and recorded two solo tackles and intercepted a pass [[Randall Cunningham]] threw to [[Randy Moss]] as the Cardinals lost 21–41.<ref>{{cite web| title=Divisional Round — Arizona Cardinals at Minnesota Vikings — January 10th, 1999 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199901020dal.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref>

====1999====
He returned as the No. 1 starting cornerback to begin the season and was paired with Corey Chavous. On September 12, 1999, Williams started in the [[1999 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals']] season-opener at the [[1999 Philadelphia Eagles season|Philadelphia Eagles]] and recorded one solo tackle, set a season-high with three pass deflections, and intercepted a pass [[Doug Pederson]] threw to wide receiver [[Torrance Small]] as they won 25–24.<ref>{{cite web| title=Arizona Cardinals at Philadelphia Eagles — September 12th, 1999 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/199909120phi.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> The following week, he set a season-high with five solo tackles during a 16–19 loss at the [[1999 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]] in Week 2. On September 27, 1999, Williams and the Cardinals appeared on nationally televised ''[[Monday Night Football]]'' against the [[1999 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]]. During the end of the second quarter, Williams unfortunately delivered the career-ending hit to Hall of Fame quarterback [[Steve Young (American football)|Steve Young]] as he threw a pass. Williams came in freely unblocked on a blindside cornerback blitz on Young after running back [[Lawrence Phillips]] failed his assignment of picking up any incoming blitzes. At the same time, cornerback [[J. J. McCleskey]] blitzed on the broadside of Young, ran by guard [[Dave Fiore]], and dove for a tackle as Young threw a pass, but would only hit Young's lower legs. With Aeneas Williams simultaneously hitting Young in the chest, the combined force would send Young falling backwards with the back of his head slamming into the turf and left Young unconscious on the field for several minutes. Young would not return after halftime and was replaced by [[Jeff Garcia]] as the 49ers defeated the Cardinals 24–10. Young suffered his fourth severe concussion from the impact in only three years and had continual symptoms of [[post-concussion syndrome]] that would immediately end his career and force his retirement.<ref>{{cite web| title=Young dealing with another concussion| url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/1999/0927/82538.html |access-date=July 11, 2025| website=ESPN.com| date=September 29, 1999}}</ref> He started in all 16 games throughout the [[1999 NFL season]] and recorded 55 combined tackles (50 solo), seven pass deflections, two interceptions, two forced fumbles, and one fumble recovery.<ref name="career"/>

====2000====
Head coach Vince Tobin retained Williams and [[Tom Knight (American football)|Tom Knight]] as the starting cornerbacks to begin the season. On October 23, 2000, the [[2000 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] fired head coach [[Vince Tobin]] after starting with a 2–5 record and appointed defensive coordinator [[Dave McGinnis]] to interim head coach for the remainder of the season. On November 5, 2000, Williams made two solo tackles, two pass deflections, and interception, and returned a fumble that linebacker [[Mark Maddox]] forced by running back [[Stephen Davis (American football)|Stephen Davis]] 104–yards for a touchdown as the Cardinals defeated the [[2000 Washington Redskins season|Washington Redskins]] 16–15.<ref>{{cite web| title=Washington Redskins at Arizona Cardinals — November 5th, 2000 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200011050crd.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> His fumble recovery returned 104–yards for a touchdown tied [[1970 Oakland Raiders season|Oakland Raiders']] [[Safety (gridiron football position)|safety]] [[Jack Tatum]] [[1972 Oakland Raiders season|(1972)]]. In Week 15, he set a season-high with six solo tackles during a 10–44 loss at the [[2000 Jacksonville Jaguars season|Jacksonville Jaguars]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Pro-Football-Reference: Aeneas Williams Game Logs (2000) |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/W/WillAe00.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> On December 24, 2000, Williams recorded six combined tackles (three solo), two pass deflections, and set a season-high with two interceptions on passes thrown by [[Brad Johnson (American football)|Brad Johnson]] during a 3–20 loss at the [[Washington Redskins]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Arizona Cardinals at Washington Redskins — December 24th, 2000 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200012240was.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> He started all 16 games throughout the [[2000 NFL season]] and finished with 62 combined tackles (48 solo), 11 pass deflections, five interceptions, two forced fumbles, two fumble recoveries, and one touchdown.<ref name="career"/>

On February 22, 2001, the [[2001 Arizona Cardinals season|Arizona Cardinals]] designated their franchise tag to Williams as both parties were still unable to reach an agreement on a contract extension. The franchise tag was for a fully-guaranteed one–year, $4.18 million contract for the [[2001 NFL season]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Bird tag stuck on Aeneas| url=https://azdailysun.com/bird-tag-stuck-on-aeneas/article_6c7002fd-ee67-5212-9bd7-599cd721db88.html |access-date=July 9, 2025 |newspaper=Arizona Daily Sun| date=February 22, 2001| last=Baum | first=Bob|language=en}}</ref>

===St. Louis Rams===
====2001====
On April 21, 2001, the [[St. Louis Rams]] traded a second (54th overall) and fourth-round pick (121st overall) in the [[2001 NFL draft]] to the [[Arizona Cardinals]] in return for Williams.<ref>[http://archive.profootballweekly.com/content/archives/features_2000/spin_042301.asp Pro Football Weekly] {{webarchive |url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060217103745/http://archive.profootballweekly.com/content/archives/features_2000/spin_042301.asp |date=February 17, 2006}}</ref> The Rams acquired Williams to replace starting cornerback [[Todd Lyght]] after he signed with the [[2001 Detroit Lions season|Detroit Lions]] ten days earlier.

On April 25, 2001, the [[2001 St. Louis Rams season|St. Louis Rams]] signed Williams to a three–year, $14.70 million contract extension that included $7.70 million guaranteed and an initial signing bonus of $3.60 million.<ref name="spotrac"/><ref>{{cite web| title=Rams acquire Aeneas Williams |url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2001-apr-22-sp-54289-story.html |access-date=July 9, 2025 |website=[[Los Angeles Times]]| date=April 22, 2001|language=en}}</ref> He entered training camp slated as the ''de facto'' No. 1 starting cornerback under defensive coordinator [[Lovie Smith]]. Head coach [[Mike Martz]] named Williams and [[Dexter McCleon]] as the starting cornerbacks to begin the season, alongside nickelback [[Dre Bly]].

On September 30, 2001, he set a season-high with eight combined tackles (seven solo) and made one fumble recovery during a 42–10 loss to the [[2001 Miami Dolphins season|Miami Dolphins]]. On October 21, 2001, Williams made eight combined tackles (five solo), one pass deflection, and returned an interception on a pass by [[Vinny Testaverde]] 42–yards for a touchdown during a 34–14 victory at the [[2001 New York Jets season|New York Jets]].<ref>{{cite web| title=St. Louis Rams at New York Jets — October 21st, 2001 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200110210nyj.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> In Week 9, he made one solo tackle, one pass deflection, and had his second pick-six of the season after intercepting a pass [[Matt Lytle]] threw to wide receiver [[Donald Hayes]] and returning it for a 16–yard touchdown during a 14–48 victory against the [[2001 Carolina Panthers season|Carolina Panthers]].<ref>{{cite web| title=Carolina Panthers at St. Louis Rams — November 11th, 2001 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200111110ram.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> In Week 13, Williams recorded four solo tackles, three pass deflections, and set a season-high with two interceptions on passes thrown by Jeff Garcia to wide receivers [[Terrell Owens]] and [[Tai Streets]] as the Rams defeated the [[2001 San Francisco 49ers season|San Francisco 49ers]] 14–27.<ref>{{cite web| title=San Francisco 49ers at St. Louis Rams — December 9th, 2001 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200112090ram.htm |access-date=July 9, 2025| website=pro-football-reference.com}}</ref> He started all 16 games for the tenth consecutive season and made 73 combined tackles (56 solo), 18 pass deflections, four forced fumbles, four interceptions, and returned two interceptions for touchdowns.<ref name="career"/>

====2003====
Due to roster concerns, Williams switched to free safety. As one of the leaders of a much-improved defense, Williams got a chance to play in the postseason for only the second time in his career. In the Rams' divisional playoff game against the [[Green Bay Packers]] prior to the Super Bowl, he returned two interceptions from Packers quarterback [[Brett Favre]] for touchdowns and recovered a fumble. Then in the NFC title game, he intercepted a pass from [[Philadelphia Eagles]] quarterback [[Donovan McNabb]], with 2 minutes left in regulation, clinching the game and ensuring the Rams' berth in [[Super Bowl XXXVI]].<ref name="f042">{{cite web | title=Aeneas Williams enjoying Super Bowl homecoming | website=Pocono Record | date=2002-02-01 | url=https://www.poconorecord.com/story/sports/pro/2002/02/01/aeneas-williams-enjoying-super-bowl/50993296007/ | access-date=2024-10-03}}</ref> However, the Rams lost that game to the [[New England Patriots]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=Super Bowl XXXVI - St. Louis Rams vs. New England Patriots - February 3rd, 2002 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/boxscores/200202030nwe.htm |access-date=2024-10-03 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref>

On March 24, 2003, the [[2003 St. Louis Rams season|St. Louis Rams]] signed Williams to a two–year, $6.50 million contract that includes a $1 million signing bonus.<ref name="spotrac"/>
====2004–2005====
After a lackluster season, in which he ended on the [[injured reserve]] list, Williams quietly retired during the 2005 offseason.<ref name="z699">{{cite web | last=Taylor | first=Betsy | title=Aeneas Williams goes from the gridiron to the pulpit | website=The State Journal-Register | date=2009-01-25 | url=https://www.sj-r.com/story/lifestyle/faith/2009/01/25/aeneas-williams-goes-from-gridiron/41742179007/ | access-date=2024-12-20}}</ref> Over his career he accumulated a staggering 12 defensive touchdowns (9 interceptions returned for a touchdown, and 3 fumbles recovered for touchdowns), and 55 career interceptions, cementing his place as one of the most dominating defensive backs of his era. He also recovered 23 fumbles and gained 1,075 total defensive return yards (807 from interceptions and 268 from fumbles). He was also a 4-time [[All-Pro]] selection.

Although Williams only played on a playoff team four times in 14 years (three of which were with the Rams), he made the most of his postseason opportunities when they occurred, intercepting 6 passes and recovering one fumble in his first four playoff games.

==Post-playing career==
Williams was inducted into the Arizona Cardinals' Ring of Honor during the 2008–2009 football season during halftime of the Monday Night Football game against the San Francisco 49ers November 10, 2008.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Williams to Ring, McKinnon to Hall |url=http://archive.azcentral.com/sports/cardinals/articles/2008/05/07/20080507cardsnews.html |website=archive.azcentral.com}}</ref> On January 18, 2009, he was chosen to present the [[NFC Championship Game#George Halas Trophy|George Halas Trophy]] to the Arizona Cardinals after their victory in the NFC Championship game, resulting in the Cardinals first trip to the Super Bowl. He made his final appearance in a football videogame in ''[[NFL Street 2]]'', which was released in 2004.

Williams is the founding pastor of The Spirit Church (formerly Spirit of the Lord Family Church), which began in 2007, located in [[St. Ann, Missouri|St. Ann]], a suburb of St. Louis.<ref>{{cite web |title=About — The Spirit Church |url=https://thespiritchurch.org/about/ |website=The Spirit Church |access-date=September 3, 2025}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |title=Pastor Aeneas Williams opens new church location in St. Ann; grand opening is 2–5 p.m. Saturday, January 27 |url=https://www.stlamerican.com/religion/local-religion/pastor-aeneas-williams-opens-new-church-location-in-st-ann/ |work=St. Louis American |date=January 24, 2018 |access-date=September 3, 2025}}</ref> He and his wife, Tracy, have three daughters—Saenea, Tirzah, and Cheyenne—and a son, Lazarus.<ref>{{Cite web |title=What's up with Aeneas Williams |url=http://archive.azcentral.com/sports/heatindex/articles/0520whatsup.html |website=azcentral.com |access-date=September 3, 2025 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150520204000/http://archive.azcentral.com/sports/heatindex/articles/0520whatsup.html |archive-date=May 20, 2015}}</ref>

Williams was a finalist for the [[Pro Football Hall of Fame]] classes of 2012 and 2013 but did not get voted in on the final ballots both times.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ex-Cardinals defensive back Aeneas Williams a finalist for Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=http://www.azcentral.com/sports/cardinals/articles/2012/01/07/20120107arizona-cardinals-aeneas-williams-hall-of-fame-finalist.html |access-date=September 6, 2012 |publisher=az central}}</ref><ref>{{Cite news |last=Corbett |first=Jim |date=February 2, 2013 |title=Parcells, Carter finally make Pro Football Hall of Fame |url=https://www.usatoday.com/story/sports/nfl/2013/02/02/nfl-hall-of-fame-announcement/1886453/ |access-date=February 2, 2013 |work=USA Today}}</ref> He was elected to the Pro Football Hall of Fame on February 1, 2014, and inducted on August 2.

On September 24, 2014, Williams was inducted into the St. Louis Sports Hall of Fame.

'''Ahman Rashad Green''' ({{IPAc-en|ɑː|ˈ|m|ɑː|n}}; born February 16, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[running back]] who played 12 seasons in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Nebraska Cornhuskers]], earning second-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] honors in 1997. Green was selected by the [[Seattle Seahawks]] in the third round of the [[1998 NFL draft]], playing there for two seasons before being traded to the [[Green Bay Packers]], with whom he played for eight of the next ten seasons. Green also played for the [[Houston Texans]], and was a four-time [[Pro Bowl]] selection with the Packers, where he holds the franchise record for rushing yards. He was the head [[esports]] coach at [[Lakeland University]] until the end of 2022.

==Early life==
Green was born in [[Omaha, Nebraska]], and attended Omaha North before transferring to [[Omaha Central High School|Omaha Central]] for high school. He was a high school All-American selection and state 'Player of the Year' as a senior.<ref name="Green's page on Huskers.com">{{cite web |url=http://www.huskers.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=100&ATCLID=1524205 |title=Ahman Green |publisher=[[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]] |access-date=November 9, 2010 |archive-date=October 24, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121024092337/http://www.huskers.com/ViewArticle.dbml?DB_OEM_ID=100&ATCLID=1524205 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

In addition to football, he also ran [[track and field]]. He currently holds the 10th fastest [[100 meters|100 meter dash]] ever in the state of Nebraska, at 10.61 seconds.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.neprepzone.com/prepzone/all-time-nebraska-high-school-track-and-field-charts/article_d0944340-0cd2-58d9-977d-8fc37989a22e.html?mode=jqm|archive-url=https://archive.today/20140901155427/http://www.neprepzone.com/prepzone/all-time-nebraska-high-school-track-and-field-charts/article_d0944340-0cd2-58d9-977d-8fc37989a22e.html?mode=jqm|url-status=dead|archive-date=September 1, 2014|title=NE Prep Zone}}</ref>

Green also competed in powerlifting in high school, placing 2nd in the ADFPA High School National [[Powerlifting]] Championships in [[Des Moines, Iowa]].

==College career==
Green was a standout running back and three-year starter at the [[University of Nebraska–Lincoln]]. He was an integral component and key contributor on two national championship squads for the [[Nebraska Cornhuskers football|Cornhuskers]].

===Freshman (1995)===
As a freshman, Green was perhaps overshadowed by his backfield mates running back [[Lawrence Phillips]] and quarterback [[Tommie Frazier]]. He was a major contributor during Nebraska's 1995 [[1996 Fiesta Bowl|championship run.]] He rushed for 1,086 yards (still the school's single-season freshman rushing record) and 13 touchdowns on 141 carries (7.7 avg.) and was honored as a freshman All-America selection by Football News. In addition, he earned Big Eight all-conference and 'Freshman of the Year' honors.<ref name="Green's page on Huskers.com" />

===Sophomore (1996)===
As a sophomore in 1996, Green compiled a team-leading 917 yards on 155 carries and seven touchdowns, despite a turf toe injury. Green had a career-high 214 yards against [[Iowa State University]] that season.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/ahman-green-1.html|title=Ahman Green College Stats|website=[[Sports Reference]]|language=en|access-date=2019-12-05}}</ref>

===Junior (1997)===
As a junior, Green garnered All-[[Big 12 Conference]] recognition and was named second-team All-America by the Associated Press and The Sporting News as Nebraska again captured the national championship. He was a finalist for the [[Doak Walker Award]], the annual honor for college football's top running back, in 1997. During that campaign he carried the ball 278 times for 1,877 yards (6.8 avg.) and 22 touchdowns (a school record for juniors). He posted 12 consecutive 100-yard games, including three contests with over 200 yards (he also had 99 yards on nine carries in the opener against Akron).

During his collegiate career, Green compiled 3,880 rushing yards and 42 touchdowns, both totals good for second place on the Cornhuskers' all-time list. He also posted 300 receiving yards and three touchdowns on 35 catches. One of Green's best collegiate performances came on January 2, 1998, in the [[Orange Bowl (game)|Orange Bowl]]. He rushed for an Orange Bowl record 206 yards and two touchdowns in Nebraska's 42–17 victory over #3 [[Tennessee Volunteers football|Tennessee]], breaking the previous 20-year-old record of 205 yards held by [[Arkansas Razorbacks football|Arkansas]] running back [[Roland Sales]]. Green was also named the [[1998 Orange Bowl]] MVP. The performance marked the Cornhuskers' record-setting third national championship in four years.

Green played in a bowl game each season he was at Nebraska. In the [[1996 Fiesta Bowl]], he rushed for 68 yards and one touchdown.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.huskermax.com/game/1995-florida-football/|title=1996 Fiesta Bowl, Nebraska vs. Florida football {{!}} HuskerMax game page|website=HuskerMax|language=en-US|access-date=2020-03-12}}</ref> In the [[1996 Orange Bowl (December)|1996 Orange Bowl]] (played at the end of the year), he rushed for 52 yards, and in the [[1998 Orange Bowl]], he rushed for 206 yards and two touchdowns.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.huskermax.com/game/1996-virginia-tech-football/|title=1996 Nebraska vs Virginia Tech football » HuskerMax game page|website=HuskerMax|language=en-US|access-date=2020-03-12}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=https://www.huskermax.com/game/1997-tennessee-football/|title=1998 Orange Bowl, Nebraska vs. Tennessee football {{!}} HuskerMax game page|website=HuskerMax|language=en-US|access-date=2020-03-12}}</ref>

===Seattle Seahawks (1998–1999)===
Green was [[NFL draft|drafted]] in the third round (76th overall) of the [[1998 NFL draft]] by the [[Seattle Seahawks]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=1998 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1998/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-29 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref> Although Green produced a high rushing average (6.0 in 1998 and 4.6 in 1999) he had difficulty earning significant playing time behind established veteran [[Ricky Watters]].

===Green Bay Packers (2000–2006)===
[[File:Ahman green.jpg|right|thumb|200px|Green with the Green Bay Packers in 2003]]
In 2000, Green was traded along with a fifth round draft pick to the [[Green Bay Packers]] for [[Fred Vinson (American football)|Fred Vinson]] and a sixth round pick.<ref name="k283">{{Cite web |last=Beacham |first=Greg |date=April 15, 2000 |title=Packers trade Vinson, draft pick to Seattle |url=https://journaltimes.com/packers-trade-vinson-draft-pick-to-seattle/article_8f1162db-3d35-52f6-a9d0-7a66c456ee41.html |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=Journal Times}}</ref> He was selected to the NFL [[Pro Bowl]] from 2001 to 2004 and broke several franchise records. From the time he joined the Packers in 2000 up through the end of the 2004 season, Green gained more yards from scrimmage (9,036) and rushing yards (6,848) than any other NFL player. Green's highest rushing touchdown per game total came in 2002, when he scored three in a 30–9 win versus the then-[[Washington Redskins]]. In 2003, he had his best year as a professional and set the Green Bay franchise record by running for 1,883 yards in the regular season, and three of his highest rushing yardage games came that season (218, 192, 176). That year, he became the first and only player in NFL history to record at least 1,850 rushing yards, average 5.0 yards per carry, score 20 touchdowns and catch 50 passes in one season. He threw a touchdown pass on October 17, [[2004 NFL season|2004]] vs. the [[Detroit Lions]].<ref>Sports Illustrated, September 24, 2007, p. 30</ref> During his time with the Packers, Green became one of two players in NFL history to have two touchdown runs of 90 or more yards ([[Bo Jackson]] is the other).<ref>{{cite web |url=https://www.espn.com/classic/s/jacksonboadd.html |title=ESPN Classic: Bo ran over Bosworth in '87 |author=Ron Flatter |publisher=ESPN |date=October 26, 2004 |access-date=September 19, 2011}}</ref> Despite his injury-shortened 2005 season, the Packers re-signed Green to a one-year, $2 million contract, with an extra $3 million in incentives. After the 2006 season he became a [[free agent]]. He signed a one-year deal to remain with the Packers.<ref name="p364">{{cite web | last=Clayton | first=John | title=Packers re-sign running back Green to one-year deal | website=ESPN.com | date=2006-03-06 | url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2355826 | access-date=2024-12-20}}</ref>

===Houston Texans (2007–2008)===
On March 4, 2007, Green signed a four-year, $23 million deal with the [[Houston Texans]].<ref name="s224">{{cite web | last=McClain | first=John | title=Texans sign running back Ahman Green | website=Chron | date=2007-03-04 | url=https://www.chron.com/sports/texans/article/texans-sign-running-back-ahman-green-1820217.php | access-date=2024-12-20}}</ref> He was reunited with his former head coach and former Texans' assistant head coach [[Mike Sherman]] along with former Packers running back [[Samkon Gado]]. He was asked to handle the bulk of the load at running back after a [[2006 NFL season|2006 season]] in which the Texans used a "running back by committee" approach.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pasquarelli |first=Len |author-link=Len Pasquarelli |date=2007-03-04 |title=Texans bolster backfield, agree with Packers' Green |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2787723 |access-date=2024-06-04 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref> Across his two seasons with the Texans, Green rushed 144 times for 554 yards and two touchdowns and also caught 25 passes for 155 yards.<ref>{{Cite web|title=Ahman Green Stats|url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GreeAh00.htm|access-date=2021-01-07|website=[[Pro Football Reference]]|language=en}}</ref>

On February 10, 2009, Green was released by the Texans.<ref name="q785">{{cite web | title=Texans release Green, Greenwood | website=Houston Texans | date=2009-02-10 | url=https://www.houstontexans.com/news/texans-release-green-greenwood-2663650 | access-date=2024-12-20}}</ref>

===Return to the Green Bay Packers (2009)===
[[File:Ahman Green scores.jpg|left|thumb|350px|Ahman Green runs in for a touchdown against Seattle on December 27, 2009.]]
Ahman Green officially re-signed with the Green Bay Packers on October 21, 2009, after the Packers placed running back DeShawn Wynn on [[Injured reserve list|injured reserve]].<ref>{{cite news|url=http://www.packers.com/news/releases/2009/10/21/1/ |work=Packers.com |title=Packers Sign RB Green, Place RB Wynn On Injured Reserve |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20091024024430/http://www.packers.com/news/releases/2009/10/21/1 |archive-date=October 24, 2009 }}</ref> With his former number, 30, taken by fullback [[John Kuhn]], Green wore No. 34, the same number as former [[Chicago Bears]] running back [[Walter Payton]], whom Green idolized as a young player.<ref name=":1">{{Cite web|date=2010-05-03|title=Packers.com » Team » Players » Ahman Green|url=http://www.packers.com/team/players/green_ahman/|access-date=2021-01-07|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100503160515/http://www.packers.com/team/players/green_ahman/|archive-date=May 3, 2010}}</ref> On November 8, 2009, Green broke Jim Taylor's record to become the all-time leading rusher in Packer history.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.yardbarker.com/nfl/articles/green_breaks_taylors_franchise_rushing_record/1526949 |title=Green Breaks Taylor's Franchise Rushing Record |work=Packers.com |date=November 8, 2009}}</ref> In his final NFL season, Green was primarily used in a reserve role, rushing 41 times for 160 yards and one touchdown and also catching 3 passes for 18 yards.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Ahman Green 2009 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GreeAh00/gamelog/2009/ |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}}</ref>

===Omaha Nighthawks (2010)===
Green joined the [[Omaha Nighthawks]] of the [[United Football League (2009)|United Football League]] for the 2010 season.<ref>{{cite news|url=http://uflaccess.com/ufl/breaking-ahman-green-to-ufl |work=UFLaccess.com |first=Billy |last=Kirk |title=Ahman Green to UFL |date=May 21, 2010 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20100528085445/http://uflaccess.com/ufl/breaking-ahman-green-to-ufl/ |archive-date=May 28, 2010 }}</ref> He was a part of the Nighthawks' 40-man protected roster, started 8 games for the Nighthawks.<ref>{{Cite web|title=History of the Omaha Nighthawks UFL Team {{!}} Omaha Nighthawks|url=https://omahanighthawks.com/|access-date=2021-01-07|language=en-US}}</ref>

===Montreal Alouettes (2011)===
On February 7, 2011, the [[Montreal Alouettes]] of the [[Canadian Football League]] announced they signed Green to a tryout contract, signing Green to an official contract in March of that year.<ref>{{cite news |url=http://www.cjad.com/blog/AlouettesNews/blogentry.aspx?BlogEntryID=10201093 |work=CJAD |first=Rick |last=Moffat |title=Als blockbuster Super Bowl weekend: Packers star signs |date=February 4, 2011}}</ref><ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cfl.ca/article/als-extend-qb-mcpherson-sign-rb-green |work=CFL.ca |title=Als extend QB McPherson, sign RB Green |date=March 9, 2011 |access-date=August 23, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20150925201420/http://www.cfl.ca/article/als-extend-qb-mcpherson-sign-rb-green |archive-date=September 25, 2015 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }}</ref> Green was released on Sunday of training camp on June 5, 2011, after arriving with an injured hamstring.<ref>{{cite news |url=https://www.cfl.ca/article/green-out-deangelis-in-at-als-training-camp |work=CFL.ca |title=Green out, DeAngelis in at Als training camp |date=June 5, 2011 |access-date=August 23, 2017 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120921071429/http://www.cfl.ca/article/green-out-deangelis-in-at-als-training-camp |archive-date=September 21, 2012 |url-status=dead |df=mdy-all }}</ref>

=== Retirement ===
Green announced his retirement from football in August 2011.<ref>{{Cite news|url=https://www.nytimes.com/2011/08/12/sports/football/ex-packer-ahman-green-retires.html|title=Ex-Packer Ahman Green Retires|agency=Associated Press|date=2011-08-11|work=The New York Times|access-date=2019-12-05|language=en-US|issn=0362-4331}}</ref>

==Personal life==
Green was named after former NFL [[wide receiver]] and current broadcaster [[Ahmad Rashad]].<ref>[http://www.ahman30.com/about.asp Ahman Green:About Green officially announced his retirement August 11th 2011.] {{webarchive|url=https://web.archive.org/web/20060824234242/http://www.ahman30.com/about.asp |date=August 24, 2006 }}</ref> He has an uncle, Michael Green, who also attended Nebraska as a running back in the late 1960s. His uncle was drafted by the [[San Diego Chargers]], but never appeared in a game.

In 2003, Green completed his undergraduate degree at Nebraska after taking classes at the [[University of Wisconsin–Green Bay]], receiving a bachelor's degree in geography.<ref name=":1" />

On September 21, 2012, Green was inducted into the University Of Nebraska Football Hall of Fame and was inducted into the Green Bay Packers Football Hall of Fame on July 19, 2014.

Green has lived in Green Bay since his retirement, and is an avid [[gamer|video-gamer]] and comic book fan – so much so that his nickname is "[[Batman]]", illustrated further by a calf tattoo of the superhero.<ref name=":1" /> He operates a sports training facility in the city, and serves as a spokesman for the Wisconsin Alzheimer's Association.<ref name=":0">{{Cite web|url=https://www.si.com/nfl/2016/12/08/nfl-green-bay-packers-ahman-green-retirement-video-games-gaming-comic-books-batman-ben-affleck|title=Q&A with Ahman Green: Gaming, Green Bay and Batman|last=Kahler|first=Kalyn|website=Sports Illustrated|language=en-us|access-date=2019-12-05}}</ref> From 2012 to 2014, Green served as co-owner of the [[Green Bay Blizzard]], an arena football team.<ref>{{Cite web|url=https://gilbertbrownfoundation.org/ahman-green/|title=Ahman Green – The Gilbert Brown Foundation|language=en-US|access-date=2019-12-05}}</ref>

In 2006, Green played a small role in the film ''[[Big Stan]]'' as the prisoner Lee Otis.<ref>[https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0490086/fullcredits#cast Big Stan Full Cast – IMDB.com], imdb.com, accessed December 27, 2011.</ref><ref>[https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2665696 Green Wants to Stay in Green Bay] ESPN.com, November 17, 2006. Accessed December 27, 2011.</ref> Green also had a small role in ''[[Batman v Superman: Dawn of Justice]]'' as an unnamed thug, but his scene was cut from the final version of the film.<ref name=":0" /><ref>{{Cite web|title=Ahman Green has a part in 'Batman v. Superman: Dawn of Justice'|url=https://www.cbssports.com/nfl/news/ahman-green-has-a-part-in-batman-v-superman-dawn-of-justice/|website=CBSSports.com|language=en|access-date=2020-05-26}}</ref>

On June 26, 2017, Green was arrested on charges of child abuse and disorderly conduct after his daughter (from a previous marriage) claimed Green pushed her and struck her in the head over a dispute about chores.<ref>[https://www.usatoday.com/story/news/2017/06/26/former-packers-running-back-ahman-green-arrested/428142001/?Former Packers running back Ahman Green arrested on suspicion of child abuse] USA Today</ref> Green eventually entered a plea bargain where he pled [[Nolo contendere|no contest]] to reduced charges of criminal damage to property and disorderly conduct, claiming that he did not want to subject his daughter to a jury trial. He received 18 months probation.<ref>{{Cite web|last=Bollier|first=Jeff|title=Former Green Bay Packers RB Ahman Green gets probation, child abuse charge dismissed|url=https://www.greenbaypressgazette.com/story/news/2018/04/19/ahman-green-probation/534490002/|access-date=2021-01-07|website=Green Bay Press-Gazette|language=en-US}}</ref>

In February 2020, Green was named head coach of [[Lakeland University]]'s new varsity [[esports]] team.<ref>[https://247sports.com/college/nebraska/Article/Nebraska-Huskers-football-Green-Bay-Packers-Ahman-Green-Esports-143675734/ Husker247 - "Ahman Green ready for a different kind of coaching"]</ref><ref>{{cite web | last=Dombeck | first=Tom | title=Esports: Green Bay Packers legend Ahman Green named Lakeland coach | website=PackersNews.com | date=2020-02-05 | url=https://www.packersnews.com/story/sports/college/2020/02/05/esports-lakeland-names-former-green-bay-packers-player-ahman-green-coach/4655135002/ | access-date=2026-04-25}}</ref>

In November 2021, Green hosted the finals of the first ever Mid-America Gamers Expo in Council Bluffs.<ref name="v320">{{cite web | last=Scheibe | first=Emmalee | title=First ever gaming expo comes to CB in November | website=Daily Nonpareil | date=2024-10-17 | url=https://nonpareilonline.com/entertainment/first-ever-gaming-expo-comes-to-cb-in-november/article_db68e76e-cca4-52be-b532-f7da9f12cd45.html | access-date=2024-10-18}}</ref>

Green was announced as a professor in the University of Nebraska–Lincoln's [[College of Journalism and Mass Communications (University of Nebraska-Lincoln)|College of Journalism and Mass Communications]] in 2023.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Wieseman |first=Connor |date=2023-03-07 |title=Four-time NFL pro bowler becomes UNL lecturer and esports coach |url=https://www.nebraskanewsservice.net/unlimitedsports/four-time-nfl-pro-bowler-becomes-unl-lecturer-and-esports-coach/article_8466e36c-218a-5607-a677-733493ab36cc.html |access-date=2025-02-11 |website=Nebraska News Service |language=en}}</ref>

'''Kabisa Akili Maradufu Smith''' (born August 21, 1975) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[quarterback]] who played in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) for four seasons with the [[Cincinnati Bengals]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Oregon Ducks football|Oregon Ducks]], winning [[Pac-12 Conference football individual awards|Pac-10 Co-Offensive Player of the Year]] and receiving first-team [[List of All-Pac-12 Conference football teams|All-Pac-10]] in 1998. Smith was selected third overall of the [[1999 NFL draft]], but his tenure was cut short by inconsistent play and questions over his work ethic. Following his departure from the Bengals in 2002, he played for the [[Frankfurt Galaxy (NFL Europe)|Frankfurt Galaxy]] of [[NFL Europe]] and the [[Calgary Stampeders]] of the [[Canadian Football League]].

==Early life==
Given the name Kabisa Akili Maradufu Smith (in [[Swahili language|Swahili]], "kabisa" means "completely", "akili" means "mind", and "maradufu" means "double" or "a Gemini twin") by his parents Glorida Bryant and Ray Smith,<ref name="Gemini">{{cite news |author=Hobson, Geoff |title=Like father, like Akili |url=http://bengals.enquirer.com/1999/04/25/ben_like_father_like.html |newspaper=[[The Cincinnati Enquirer]] |date=April 25, 1999 |access-date=2017-04-02 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170404043525/http://bengals.enquirer.com/1999/04/25/ben_like_father_like.html |archive-date=April 4, 2017 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Akili Smith was born in [[San Diego|San Diego, California]]. Smith attended [[Lincoln High School (San Diego, California)|Abraham Lincoln High School]] in San Diego, the alma mater of [[Marcus Allen]] and [[Terrell Davis]].<ref name="lhh001">{{cite web|url=http://weblog.signonsandiego.com/multimedia/utmedia/070902lincoln/index.html |title=Special Feature on Lincoln High School's History |publisher=San Diego Union-Tribune |access-date=2007-09-28 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20090303145027/http://weblog.signonsandiego.com/multimedia/utmedia/070902lincoln/index.html |archive-date=March 3, 2009 }}</ref>

Smith was named a [[Parade Magazine]] All-American and signed a letter of intent to play football at [[San Diego State]], but low test scores prevented him from enrolling there to play football.<ref name="Gemini"/>

Smith was drafted by the [[Pittsburgh Pirates]] in the seventh round (206th overall) of the [[1993 Major League Baseball draft]]. He played for the [[Gulf Coast League Pirates]] of the [[Gulf Coast League]] from 1993 to 1994, and the [[Erie SeaWolves]] of the [[New York–Penn League]] in 1995.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.baseball-reference.com/register/player.fcgi?id=smith-001kab | title=Akili Smith | publisher=[[Baseball Reference]] | accessdate=17 March 2026}}</ref>

==College career==

===Grossmont College===
After he was unable to play at San Diego State, Smith attended [[Grossmont College]], a [[junior college]] in the San Diego area, for two years.<ref name="Gemini"/> At Grossmont, he played under head coach Dave Jordan. Over his junior college career, Smith threw 49 touchdown passes and 18 interceptions, and he became one of the top junior-college quarterback recruits in the country.<ref name="ESPNDraft">{{cite web |title=Smith hopes NFL pays off on big gamble |url=https://a.espncdn.com/nfl/s/1999/0423/30705.html |publisher=[[ESPN]] |date=April 23, 1999 |access-date=June 5, 2026}}</ref>

===Oregon===
Smith transferred to the [[University of Oregon]], where he played for the [[Oregon Ducks football|Oregon Ducks]] under head coach [[Mike Bellotti]]. He joined the Ducks in 1997 and shared quarterback duties with [[Jason Maas]]. In his first season at Oregon, Smith completed 104 of 190 passes for 1,298 yards, 12 touchdowns, and six interceptions, while also rushing for 195 yards and two touchdowns.<ref name="Oregon1997">{{cite web |title=1997 Oregon Ducks Stats |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/oregon/1997.html |website=[[Sports Reference|Sports-Reference.com]] |access-date=June 5, 2026}}</ref>

As a senior in 1998, Smith became one of the most productive quarterbacks in Oregon history. In the regular season, he completed 191 of 325 passes for 3,307 yards, 30 touchdowns, and seven interceptions, while leading the [[Pacific-10 Conference]] in passing yards and touchdown passes.<ref name="Oregon1998">{{cite web |title=1998 Oregon Ducks Stats |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/schools/oregon/1998.html |website=[[Sports Reference|Sports-Reference.com]] |access-date=June 5, 2026}}</ref> He also led the NCAA in passing yards per attempt.<ref name="ESPNDraft"/>

Including Oregon's [[Aloha Bowl]] appearance against [[1998 Colorado Buffaloes football team|Colorado]], Smith finished the 1998 season with 3,763 passing yards, 32 touchdown passes, and eight interceptions on 371 attempts. He also recorded 3,947 yards of total offense.<ref name="Oregon1998PDF">{{cite web |title=1998 Oregon Football Statistics |url=https://goducks.com/documents/download/2022/7/28/1998.pdf |publisher=[[Oregon Ducks]] |access-date=June 5, 2026}}</ref> Smith was named second-team [[All-America college football team|All-American]] and [[Pac-12 Conference football individual awards|Pac-10 Conference Co-Offensive Player of the Year]].<ref name="ESPNDraft"/><ref name="Pac10Awards">{{cite web |title=Pac-12 Offensive Player of the Year Winners |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/awards/pac-12-opoy.html |website=[[Sports Reference|Sports-Reference.com]] |access-date=June 5, 2026}}</ref> His senior season helped move him into consideration as one of the top quarterback prospects for the [[1999 NFL draft]].<ref name="ESPNDraft"/>

===Cincinnati Bengals===
In the [[1999 NFL draft]], a year in which five quarterbacks were drafted in the first round, Smith was the third quarterback and third player selected overall, by the [[Cincinnati Bengals]]. Smith scored a 16 out of 50 on the NFL-administered [[Wonderlic test]] when he first took the exam in 1998. His agent [[Leigh Steinberg]] hired a tutor to help improve his score for the 1999 scouting combine, and he scored a 37 on the second try.<ref name="Gemini"/>

Prior to the draft, there was an effort by [[New Orleans Saints]]' [[head coach]] [[Mike Ditka]] and management to get the Cincinnati Bengals' high draft position so the Saints could get [[Ricky Williams]]. The final offer, which was refused by Bengals management, was for nine draft picks, several extra in that year as well as many the next year. Instead of taking the trade, the Bengals stayed with their initial decision to draft Smith,<ref>{{Cite web |title=1999 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/1999/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-28 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> who, while athletic (he had also played two years of minor-league baseball and ran a 4.66 [[40-yard dash]]<ref name="Draft scout">{{cite web|url=http://www.nfldraftscout.com/ratings/dsprofile.php?pyid=61119&draftyear=1999&genpos=QB|title=Akili Smith, DS #4 QB, Oregon|work=NFLDraftScout.com|access-date=2009-01-16}}</ref>), was still largely unproven, having only succeeded at the college level for one season.

Smith missed a large portion of [[National Football League training camp|training camp]] during his rookie season in [[1999 NFL season|1999]] due to contract disputes. On August 24, 1999, he signed a seven-year contract worth up to $56 million with a $10.8 million [[signing bonus]].<ref>{{cite news |author=Sullivan, Tim |title=Big payday could be Akili's heel |url=http://enquirer.com/editions/1999/08/25/spt_big_payday_could_be.html |newspaper=[[The Cincinnati Enquirer]] |date=August 25, 1999 |access-date=2017-04-02}}</ref>

Despite showing athleticism in his early games, he failed to grasp the Bengals playbook fully and never established himself with the team. His [[offensive coordinator]] from 2001 to 2002, [[Bob Bratkowski]], said Smith "wasn't as diligent as he should have been" regarding his film and playbook study habits.<ref name="hindsight">{{cite news |author=Sullivan, Tim |title=A decade of hindsight guides former NFL QB Akili Smith |url=http://www.sandiegouniontribune.com/sdut-chargers-sullivan-akili-smith205216-2009apr25-story.html |newspaper=[[The San Diego Union-Tribune]] |date=April 25, 2009 |access-date=2017-04-02}}</ref>  During the four years he was with the Bengals, he started in only 17 games and threw just five touchdown passes and 13 interceptions, eventually leading to his release on May 31, 2003, after riding the bench mostly during the previous two years.

===Later career===
In [[2003 NFL season|2003]], Smith tried out for the [[Green Bay Packers]], as [[Brett Favre]]'s backup. He was, however, unsuccessful there and was later released.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=1603429|title=Tight end Tyrone Davis also released|work=[[ESPN.com]]|publisher=[[ESPN]]|date=August 26, 2003}}</ref> In 2005, he was released by the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]] after a stint in [[NFL Europa|NFL Europe]] where he started four games for the [[Frankfurt Galaxy (NFL Europe)|Frankfurt Galaxy]].

On April 28, [[2007 CFL season|2007]], Smith signed a two-year contract with the [[Calgary Stampeders]] of the [[Canadian Football League]], where he was expected to compete for the starting quarterback position with another former NFL player, [[Henry Burris]].<ref>{{cite news |author=Pasquarelli, Len |title=Smith, out of NFL for two years, signs in CFL |url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2852141 |website=ESPN.com |date=April 28, 2007 |access-date=2017-04-02}}</ref> After an unimpressive debut in an [[exhibition game]] against the [[Edmonton Eskimos]], Smith played well in the final exhibition against the [[Saskatchewan Roughriders]]. Though listed going into the game as the third-string [[quarterback]], he completed three [[touchdown]] passes in only one half of play, including one to former [[Kansas City Chiefs]] [[wide receiver]] [[Marc Boerigter]].

==Post-football career==
After retiring from football, Smith was the quarterbacks coach for [[Grossmont College]].<ref name="hindsight"/> Smith was a [[deacon]] at a [[Missionary Baptist]] church and played football for "God's House", a [[flag football]] team.<ref>''Sports Illustrated'', July 2009, "Where Are They Now?: Akili Smith"</ref>

In March 2010, Smith joined the [[California Golden Bears football|California Golden Bears]]'s football staff as a graduate assistant to work with the offense. Cal head coach [[Jeff Tedford]] previously coached Smith at Oregon when he was offensive coordinator.<ref>{{cite news |date=March 13, 2010 |title=Smith hired to work with offense |url=http://www.espn.com/ncf/news/story?id=4992741 |access-date=2017-04-02 |website=ESPN.com|agency=Associated Press}}</ref>

In 2012, Smith took over as quarterbacks coach for [[St. Augustine High School (San Diego)|St. Augustine High School]] in [[San Diego]].<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.utsandiego.com/news/2012/nov/05/st-augustine-receives-boost-former-nfl-quarterback/?print&page=all|title=St. Augustine receives boost from former NFL quarterback|access-date=2012-11-05}}</ref> Smith planned to finish the college degree that he started at the University of Oregon.<ref>{{cite web | last=Olivieri | first=Anthony | title=Former draft bust Akili Smith has a surprising new path | website=Yahoo! Sports | date=2012-04-12 | url=https://sports.yahoo.com/blogs/nfl-shutdown-corner/former-draft-bust-akili-smith-surprising-path-185754242.html?guccounter=1 | access-date=2025-08-20}}</ref> As of September 2014, Smith was coaching football for [[The Bishop's School (La Jolla)|The Bishop's School]] in [[La Jolla]], [[California]], and was still 16 credits away from graduating from Oregon.<ref>{{cite news |author=Greif, Andrew |title=Former Oregon Ducks quarterback Akili Smith on Marcus Mariota: 'The kid is absolutely flawless' |url=https://www.oregonlive.com/ducks/2014/09/former_oregon_ducks_quarterbac_3.html |website=OregonLive.com |date=September 12, 2014 |access-date=May 25, 2019}}</ref>

In June 2020, Smith was hired onto the coaching staff at [[Maranatha High School]] in Pasadena, California.<ref>{{cite web  | title=Former NFL Quarterback Akili Smith Joins Football Staff at Maranatha High School| website=Pasadena Now | date=June 22, 2020 | url=https://pasadenanow.com/main/former-nfl-quarterback-akili-smith-joins-football-staff-at-maranatha | access-date=2025-08-20}}</ref>
