'''Ahmed Kamil Plummer''' (born March 26, 1976) is an American former  professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] for six seasons with the [[San Francisco 49ers]] of the [[National Football League]] (NFL) from 2000 to 2005. Standing 5'11" and 191 lb. from [[Ohio State University]]<!--Wikipedians do not use "The" as part of Ohio State's name; it is considered a marketing gimmick, and routinely deleted.-->, Plummer was selected by the 49ers in the first round (24th overall) in the [[2000 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |title=2000 NFL Draft Listing |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2000/draft.htm |access-date=2023-03-19 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> After only playing in 9 of the last 32 games due to injuries and missing significant parts of both 2004 and 2005 seasons, he announced his retirement from the NFL on June 16, 2006.<ref>{{Cite web |last=Pasquarelli |first=Len |author-link=Len Pasquarelli |date=2006-06-17 |title=Ex-49ers standout cornerback Plummer to retire |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=2488553 |access-date=2023-11-20 |website=ESPN.com |language=en}}</ref>

Plummer is the [[cousin]] of former [[National Basketball Association|NBA]] player, [[Brian Grant]].

'''Ahmad Rashad Merritt''' (born February 5, 1977) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[wide receiver]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Wisconsin Badgers football|Wisconsin Badgers]] and was signed by the [[Chicago Bears]] as an [[undrafted free agent]] in 2000.

Merritt was a member of the [[Dallas Cowboys]], [[Chicago Rush]] and [[Arizona Cardinals]].

==Early life==
Merritt was born in Chicago and named after former NFL running back and wide receiver [[Ahmad Rashad]], who was his father's favorite player at the time.  Merritt attended [[St. Rita of Cascia High School|St. Rita High School]] on Chicago's south side, where, as a senior, he earned All-America honors from ''[[Prep Football Report]]'' and ''[[SuperPrep]]''.  He had 63 receptions for 1,240 yards and 23 touchdowns throughout his high school career.  Merritt was a grade school, high school, and college teammate of former NFL player [[Tony Simmons (wide receiver)|Tony Simmons]].  Merritt and Simmons both played and caught touchdown passes in [[World Bowl IX]].  In 2012, Merritt was inducted into the St. Rita High School Hall of Fame.

==College career==
Merritt started 21 games at wide receiver but primarily served as a return specialist through his four years at Wisconsin.  He finished his collegiate career with 36 receptions for 528 yards and two touchdowns, 28 kick returns for 521 yards and 25 punt returns for 165 yards.

==Professional career==

===Chicago Bears===
Merritt is probably most remembered for his 47-yard [[touchdown]] run on a reverse in the Bears 2001 [[NFL playoffs, 2001-02#NFC: Philadelphia Eagles 33, Chicago Bears 19|divisional playoff]] loss to the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] (the last offensive touchdown scored for the Bears in Old [[Soldier Field]]).<ref>https://www.espn.com/nfl/playoffs01/news/2002/0119/1314280.html</ref>  He was also the leading receiver of the 2001 [[World Bowl]] Champion [[Berlin Thunder]] of [[NFL Europa]].

===Dallas Cowboys===
Merritt was in training camp with the [[Dallas Cowboys]] in 2005 and was on the verge of securing a roster spot when he tore [[ligament]]s in his foot and was given an injury settlement.  He returned to the Cowboys in the offseason, but was later released a few days into training camp before the [[2006 NFL season|2006 season]].

===Chicago Rush===
Merritt started the first five games of the 2007 Arena Football season for the [[Chicago Rush]], gaining 203 yards on 20 receptions with two touchdowns before being waived in early April.

===Arizona Cardinals===
Merritt was signed as a free agent by the [[Arizona Cardinals]] but spent his entire first season with the team on injured reserved after dislocating his ankle and breaking his fibula in a preseason game against the [[Houston Texans]].  He was re-signed by the team on March 26, 2008; however, he was released prior to the season on August 20.

{{Short description|American football player and sportscaster (born 1949)}} {{Use American English|date=February 2026}} {{Use mdy dates|date=July 2023}} {{Infobox NFL biography | name = Ahmad Rashad | image = Ahmad Rashad (4x5 cropped).jpg | alt = Head and shoulders photograph of Rashad wearing a blue baseball cap bearing the Oregon Ducks logo | caption = Rashad in 2009 | number = 28, 27 | position = [[Wide receiver]] | birth_date = {{Birth date and age|1949|11|19|mf=y}} | birth_place = [[Portland, Oregon]], U.S. | death_date = | death_place = | height_ft = 6 | height_in = 2 | weight_lb = 205 | high_school = [[Mount Tahoma High School|Mount Tahoma]]
([[Tacoma, Washington]]) | college = [[Oregon Ducks football|Oregon]] (1968–1971) | draftyear = 1972 | draftround = 1 | draftpick = 4 | pastteams = * [[St. Louis Cardinals (NFL)|St. Louis Cardinals]] ({{NFL Year|1972|1973}}) * [[Buffalo Bills]] ({{NFL Year|1974|1975}}) * [[Minnesota Vikings]] ({{NFL Year|1976|1982}}) | highlights = * Second-team [[All-Pro]] ([[1979 All-Pro Team|1979]]) * 4× [[Pro Bowl]] ([[1979 Pro Bowl|1978]]–[[1982 Pro Bowl|1981]]) * [[Minnesota Vikings#50 Greatest Vikings (2010)|50 Greatest Vikings]] * [[Minnesota Vikings Ring of Honor]] * [[Minnesota Vikings 25th Anniversary Team]] * [[Minnesota Vikings 40th Anniversary Team]] * First-team [[College Football All-America Team|All-American]] ([[1971 College Football All-America Team|1971]]) * 3× First-team [[List of All-Pac-12 Conference football teams|All-Pac-8]] ([[1969 All-Pacific-8 Conference football team|1969]], [[1970 All-Pacific-8 Conference football team|1970]], [[1971 All-Pacific-8 Conference football team|1971]]) | statlabel1 = [[Reception (gridiron football)|Receptions]] | statvalue1 = 495 | statlabel2 = [[Receiving yards]] | statvalue2 = 6,831 | statlabel3 = [[Touchdown|Receiving touchdowns]] | statvalue3 = 44 | pfr = RashAh00 | CollegeHOF = 2200 }} '''Ahmad Rashad''' ({{IPAc-en|ə|ˈ|m|ɑː|d|_|r|ə|ˈ|ʃ|ɑː|d}} {{respell|ə|MAHD|_|rə|SHAHD}}; born '''Robert Earl Moore'''; November 19, 1949) is an American [[sportscaster]] and former professional [[American football|football]] [[wide receiver]]. He was the fourth overall selection of the [[1972 NFL draft]], taken by the [[1972 St. Louis Cardinals (NFL) season|St. Louis Cardinals]]. He was known as '''Bobby Moore''' before changing his name in 1973. Recruited after high school as a wide receiver by the [[University of Oregon]], he played for the [[Oregon Ducks football|Oregon Ducks]]. He moved to the [[running back]] position and was named to the [[1971 College Football All-America Team]] at that position. He became professional after being drafted by the Cardinals. Rashad returned to playing as wide receiver, and played for the Cardinals for two seasons. After being traded to the [[Buffalo Bills]] in 1974, and sitting out the 1975 season with a knee injury, he signed with the [[Seattle Seahawks]] before the 1976 season. They traded him shortly thereafter to the [[Minnesota Vikings]] (1976–1982), where he earned four [[Pro Bowl]] selections from [[1978 NFL season|1978]] to [[1981 NFL season|1981]]. Following his retirement from football, Rashad transitioned to television. He worked as a studio analyst, game reporter, and anchor for several sports. Rashad was a panellist on the [[The NFL on NBC pregame show|NFL Live]] pregame show for NBC, and also notably hosted the [[National Basketball Association]] weekly digest shows ''[[NBA Inside Stuff]]'' ([[1990–91 NBA season|1990]]–[[2003–04 NBA season|2004]]) and ''NBA Access with Ahmad Rashad'' ([[2005–06 NBA season|2005]]–[[2010–11 NBA season|2011]]). He has appeared as a fictionalized version of himself as a television sports personality in several films and television shows. In addition, he has hosted several non-sports related game shows and reality television shows. {{As of|2021}}, he was a member of the digital content team for the [[New York Knicks]], filming videos for their YouTube channel, as well as emceeing events for the team in [[Madison Square Garden]]. ==Early life== Born Robert Earl Moore in 1949 in [[Portland, Oregon]], he moved with his family to [[Tacoma, Washington]]. There he played [[high school football]]. Rashad graduated from [[Mount Tahoma High School]]{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=6ZJYAAAAIBAJ&pg=4322%2C3280982 |newspaper=Spokane Daily Chronicle |location=Washington |title=Moore exciting coaches and fans |date=October 27, 1971 |page=31 }} and accepted an [[athletic scholarship]] to the [[University of Oregon]] in [[Eugene, Oregon|Eugene]]. He played [[College football|football]] for the [[Oregon Ducks football|Ducks]] under head coach [[Jerry Frei]], became a member of [[Omega Psi Phi]] [[Fraternities and sororities|fraternity]], and majored in elementary education at Oregon.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=HVlUAAAAIBAJ&pg=7063%2C1418749 |newspaper=Ellensburg Daily Record |location=Washington |agency=UPI |title=Moore 4th pick |date=February 1, 1972 |page=7}} During his junior year in college, Rashad had legal issues in Portland. He was charged with [[felony]] theft in November 1970.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=H-dVAAAAIBAJ&pg=2822%2C1003984 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |title=Moore facing Portland theft attempt charge |date=November 4, 1970 |page=1D }}{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=IOdVAAAAIBAJ&pg=6231%2C1178933 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon|last=Cawood |first=Neil |title=Bobby Moore suspended for Air Force-Oregon battle |date=November 5, 1970 |page=1C }}{{cite news |url= https://news.google.com/newspapers?nid=1310&dat=19701123&id=MudVAAAAIBAJ&pg=3798,5808542&hl=en |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |title=Moore bound to grand jury |date=November 23, 1970 |page=1C }} He pleaded guilty to a reduced charge, a [[misdemeanor]], in early 1971.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=aeVVAAAAIBAJ&pg=3889%2C870264 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |title=UO's Moore on probation for one year |date=January 5, 1971 |page=3B }} In 1972, Moore converted from [[Pentecostalism]] to [[Quranism|Islam]]. He had started to study Islam in college.{{cite book| first= William J. |last= Baker|title=Playing With God: Religion and Modern Sport|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Brpa5FYhK7MC&q=ahmad%20rashad%20islam&pg=PA227|publisher=Harvard University Press|access-date=December 26, 2014|page=227|date=2007|isbn= 9780674020443}} A year later, Bobby Moore legally changed his name to Ahmad Rashād, which means "admirable one led to truth" in Arabic.{{cite news|url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=ZVZYAAAAIBAJ&pg=3771%2C4725582 |newspaper=The Bulletin |location=Bend, Oregon|title=Bobby Moore has changed more than name |agency=Associated Press |date=October 23, 1973 |page=10 }} He adopted his last name from his Egyptian-American mentor, biochemist [[Rashad Khalifa]],{{cite news|first= Paul |last= Brownfield| url= https://www.nytimes.com/2013/01/02/sports/baseball/sam-khalifa-briefly-a-rising-star-forever-a-mourning-son.html |title= Briefly a Rising Star, Forever a Mourning Son| work= The New York Times |access-date= February 17, 2013 |date= January 2, 2013}} with whom he studied Arabic.{{cite news| last= Olderman| first= Murray| title= Rashad made a name for himself...twice |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=GrgdAAAAIBAJ&pg=1963%2C3707744| newspaper= Pittsburgh Press|date=July 26, 1981 |page=D-2}} Khalifa was assassinated in 1990. ==Football career== At Oregon, Moore played [[wide receiver]] and wingback as a sophomore in [[1969 Oregon Ducks football team|1969]] and made the [[1969 All-Pacific-8 Conference football team|all-conference team]].{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=6PBVAAAAIBAJ&pg=5663%2C7292801|newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon|title=Bobby Moore all Pacific-8|date=November 30, 1969 |page=1B}} He moved to running back, where he was an [[1971 College Football All-America Team|All-American]] in [[1971 Oregon Ducks football team|1971]]—in the same backfield with [[quarterback]] [[Dan Fouts]]. In his final season with the Ducks (1971), he rushed for 1,211 yards, caught 32 passes for 324 yards, and scored 10 touchdowns. He finished his three seasons of college football with 2,036 rushing yards, 131 receptions for 1,565 yards, and 36 touchdowns.{{Cite web |title=Bobby Moore College Stats, School, Draft, Gamelog, Splits |url=https://www.sports-reference.com/cfb/players/bobby-moore-2.html |access-date=2024-12-20 |website=College Football at Sports-Reference.com |language=en}} At the time Moore left Oregon, his rushing yards, receptions, and 226 points were all school records.{{Cite web|url=https://goducks.com/honors/hall-of-fame/ahmad-rashad/165|title = Ahmad Rashad (1992) – Hall of Fame}} Moore was the fourth player selected in the [[1972 NFL draft]], taken by the [[1972 St. Louis Cardinals (NFL) season|St. Louis Cardinals]].{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=rdtVAAAAIBAJ&pg=6395%2C72254 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard|location=Oregon|title=Moore, Drougas taken in first round |date=February 1, 1972 |page=1B }} He made the UPI all-rookie team in [[1972 NFL season|1972]],{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=NqlVAAAAIBAJ&pg=6553%2C6311441 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard |location=Oregon |agency=UPI |title=Three ex-Ducks get rookie spots |date=December 24, 1972 |page=4B }} but second-year head coach [[Bob Hollway]] was fired after a 4–9–1 season. [[Don Coryell]] was the new head coach in [[1973 St. Louis Cardinals (NFL) season|1973]]. He traded Rashad, as he was then known, after that season to the [[1974 Buffalo Bills season|Buffalo Bills]] for backup quarterback [[Dennis Shaw]].{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=9DYyAAAAIBAJ&pg=5329%2C5365818 |newspaper=Palm Beach Post |agency=Associated Press |title=Cards get Bills' Shaw |date=January 27, 1974 |page=E2 }}{{Dead link|date=September 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }} In Buffalo, Rashad roomed on the road with [[O. J. Simpson]] in [[1974 Buffalo Bills season|1974]]. He missed the [[1975 Buffalo Bills season|1975]] season after a knee injury in the final pre-season game.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=0atVAAAAIBAJ&pg=3875%2C5125130 |newspaper=Eugene Register-Guard|location=Oregon|agency=Associated Press |last=Baker |first=Tony |title=Rashad is on the road back |date=July 21, 1976 |page=3B }} Rashad was in the training camp of the expansion [[1976 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]], after signing as a free agent. He was traded days before the start of the [[1976 NFL season|1976]] regular season, sent to the [[1976 Minnesota Vikings season|Minnesota Vikings]] for a future draft pick.{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=nrESAAAAIBAJ&pg=1931%2C1518342 |newspaper=Spokane Daily Chronicle|location=Washington |agency=Associated Press |title=Rashad dealt by Seahawks; Picard placed on waivers |date=September 8, 1976 |page=19}} He failed the Vikings' physical, but was kept on the team due to the actions of quarterback [[Fran Tarkenton]].{{cite news |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=GrgdAAAAIBAJ&pg=1963%2C3707744 |newspaper=Pittsburgh Press |last=Olderman |first=Murray |title=Rashad made a name for himself...twice |date=July 26, 1981 |page=D-2 }} The Vikings made it back to the [[Super Bowl XI|Super Bowl]] that season, their last appearance to date. During his professional football career, Rashad caught 495 passes for 6,831 yards and 44 touchdowns, while also rushing for 52 yards. The standout catch of his career came in a December [[1980 Minnesota Vikings season|1980]] game against the [[1980 Cleveland Browns season|Cleveland Browns]]. Vikings quarterback [[Tommy Kramer]] threw a [[Hail Mary pass]] to Rashad that resulted in a come-from-behind 28–23 victory and a [[NFC North|Central Division]] title for the Vikings. This became known as "The [[Miracle at the Met]]", or, alternatively, "The Miracle Catch". Rashad also has the distinction of the longest play from scrimmage that didn't score a touchdown: 98 yards in a 1972 game against the Rams. Rashad replaced [[John Gilliam]] as receiver with both the St. Louis and Minnesota teams. In 1992 Rashad was named to Oregon's Hall of Fame and to the [[College Football Hall of Fame]] on May 9, 2007.{{College Football HoF|id=2200|name=Ahmad Rashād}} ==Broadcasting and television career== {{See also|NFL on NBC|NBA on NBC|NBA on ABC}} After his football career, Rashad covered [[National Football League|NFL]], [[National Basketball Association|NBA]], and [[Major League Baseball|MLB]]{{YouTube|title=1987 04 25 NBC GOW Baltimore Orioles at Milwaukee Brewers|id=4F3kNvXkftU}} televised contests as a studio anchor and game reporter for [[NBC Sports|NBC]] and [[ESPN on ABC|ABC]], and hosted ''[[NBA Inside Stuff]]'' for 16 seasons. He also has hosted the video-clip show ''[[Real TV]]'' in 2000, the reality show ''[[The Mole (American TV series)|Celebrity Mole]]'', the [[game show]] ''[[Caesars Challenge]]'' along with co-host Dan Doherty, ''NBA Access with Ahmad Rashad'' on the ABC network, and the first season of [[Game Show Network]]'s ''[[Tug of Words]]''. [[Samantha Harris]] replaced him for the second season of ''Tug of Words''.{{Cite web |title=Ahmad Rashad |url=https://www.tvguide.com/celebrities/ahmad-rashad/credits/3030394585/ |access-date=2023-10-06 |website=TVGuide.com |language=en}}{{Citation |last=Rick Rosner Productions |title=Caesar's Challenge {{!}} Babette/Mike/Heather |date=1993 |url=http://archive.org/details/caesarschallenge-babettemikeheather |access-date=2023-10-06}} He starred in an episode of ''[[Monsters (American TV series)|Monsters]]''. Rashad has also guest starred on several TV shows, mainly ones that starred his then-wife Phylicia Allen Rashad. In 1988, he filled in for [[Robb Weller]] on the weekend edition of ''[[Entertainment Tonight]]'' (then known as ''Entertainment This Week''). He used to interview long-time friend [[Michael Jordan]] frequently while he was at NBC. In early 2013, he became a panelist on the daily talk show ''Morning Drive'' on the [[Golf Channel]], but left that summer. Rashad has narrated the yearly highlight films for NBA championship teams since 2012. As of May 2021, Rashad now works for the [[New York Knicks]] as a member of their digital content team, making videos for the team's YouTube channel (including sit-down interviews with members of the roster as well as historical retrospectives) as well as emceeing events for the team at [[Madison Square Garden]].{{cite web | last=Best | first=Neil | title=Ahmad Rashad joining Knicks' digital content team | website=Newsday | date=2021-05-06 | url=https://www.newsday.com/sports/media/ahmad-rashad-knicks-digital-content-e20094 | access-date=2024-12-20}} == Basketball career == Right before the launch of NBA Inside Stuff in 1990, Rashad, who was 40 years old at the time, signed a two-day contract with the [[Philadelphia 76ers]].{{Cite web|last=Moore|first=Kevin|date=2020-10-17|title=Ahmad Rashad Did the Unthinkable and Played in an NBA Preseason Game|url=https://www.sportscasting.com/ahmad-rashad-did-the-unthinkable-and-played-in-an-nba-preseason-game/|access-date=2022-01-07|website=Sportscasting {{!}} Pure Sports|language=en-US|archive-date=January 8, 2022|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20220108224934/https://www.sportscasting.com/ahmad-rashad-did-the-unthinkable-and-played-in-an-nba-preseason-game/|url-status=dead}} As the show wanted to use Rashad playing in the NBA as a promotion, he was allowed to practice with the team and play in an [[Preseason friendly|NBA preseason game]] against the [[Minnesota Timberwolves]] the next day. Rashad was known for his athleticism, as evidenced by him playing multiple offensive positions in his football career. He became a multi-sport athlete, albeit 8 years after his retirement from pro sports. It was the first preseason game ever to be played at the newly built [[Target Center]] and was in front of a crowd of 18,296. Many fans came to the game to support Rashad because of his career as a Viking. He was subbed on for [[Hersey Hawkins]] and, in the first play of his NBA career, he gave up an [[Foul (basketball)|and-one shooting foul]] to [[Tony Campbell]]. During an ensuing timeout, head coach [[Jim Lynam]] drew up a play for Rashad to run across the [[Basketball court|baseline]] for an open look. Rashad knocked down the 20-foot shot and scored the first and only points of his NBA career. Remembering the moment in a voiceover, Rashad was ecstatic, "I definitely replayed this one in my head for quite some time. My teammates set me up on the left side, and when everything was on the line, I nailed it."{{Citation|title=Ahmad Rashad Plays Game For Sixers‼️| date=November 21, 2016 |url=https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=aele5Yxn5a0|language=en|access-date=2022-01-07}} Rashad was not as good defensively, as he allowed Campbell and the Timberwolves to bring an 11-point deficit down to 5. But the 76ers pulled off a 102–96 win, giving Rashad a perfect record in the NBA, as well as a perfect 1.000 FG%, as he technically made every single shot he ever took.{{Cite web|last=Astramskas|first=David|title=Remember When The NBA Let Former NFL Player & TV Host Ahmad Rashad Play In A NBA Game?|url=https://ballislife.com/remember-when-the-nba-let-former-nfl-player-tv-host-ahmad-rashad-play-in-a-nba-game/|access-date=2022-01-07|website=ballislife.com|date=April 12, 2017 |language=en-US}}{{Cite web |title=Remember When The NBA Let Former NFL Player & TV Host Ahmad Rashad Play In A NBA Game? |url=https://ballislife.com/remember-when-the-nba-let-former-nfl-player-tv-host-ahmad-rashad-play-in-a-nba-game/ |access-date=2024-02-26 |website=ballislife.com |date=April 12, 2017 |language=en-US}} After the game, Rashad's performance was applauded by multiple teammates and coaches, including [[Naismith Memorial Basketball Hall of Fame|Hall of Fame]] teammate [[Charles Barkley]]. He had previously expressed doubts about Rashad, but said that "he made it, and that's all that matters." [[Rick Mahorn]], another teammate, said "What the hell, his two points really made a difference." '''Akbar Oluwakemi-Idowu Gbajabiamila'''{{audio|LL-Q34311 (yor)-Abike25-Akbar Oluwakemi-Idowu Gbajabiamila.wav|listen}}(named in some sources as '''Gbaja-Biamila''', born May 6, 1979)<ref>{{Cite web |title=Akbar Gbaja-Biamila Career Stats - NFL |url=https://www.espn.com/nfl/player/stats/_/id/4942/akbar-gbaja-biamila |access-date=2024-05-28 |website=ESPN |language=en}}</ref> is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player in the [[National Football League]] (NFL) who is a commentator and co-host of ''[[American Ninja Warrior]]'' and its spin-off ''[[American Ninja Warrior Junior]]''. He is also an analyst for the [[NFL Network]], co-hosting the flagship morning show ''[[Good Morning Football]]'' (and syndicated spin-off/extension show ''Good Morning Football: Overtime'') and was a co-host of ''[[The Talk (talk show)|The Talk]]'' on [[CBS]] from 2021 to 2024.

Gbajabiamila is Nigerian-American and grew up in the [[Crenshaw, Los Angeles|Crenshaw]] district of Los Angeles with his mother and father, both of whom were born and raised in [[Nigeria]], and his six siblings. Among his siblings is former [[Green Bay Packers]] [[defensive end]] [[Kabeer Gbaja-Biamila]]. Before starting his professional career, Gbajabiamila played [[college football]] for the [[San Diego State Aztecs football|San Diego State Aztecs]]. He was signed by the [[Oakland Raiders]] as an undrafted free agent in 2003. Gbajabiamila played for two other teams, the [[San Diego Chargers]] and [[Miami Dolphins]].

Gbajabiamila is also an author, having released his first book, ''Everyone Can Be a Ninja'' on May 7, 2019.

==Early life==
Akbar Oluwakemi-Idowu Gbajabiamila was born on May 6, 1979, in [[Los Angeles]], [[California]], to Nigerian immigrant parents. He is one of seven children.<ref name="USANetwork">{{cite web |title=Akbar Gbaja-Biamila |url=https://www.usanetwork.com/american-ninja-warrior-ninja-vs-ninja/credits/host/akbar-gbajabiamila |publisher=USA Network |access-date=September 20, 2024}}</ref> He grew up in [[Crenshaw, Los Angeles|Crenshaw District]], and attended [[Crenshaw High School]] in [[South Los Angeles]], where he was a star basketball player on teams that were part of the Willie West Jr. coaching era.<ref name="USANetwork" /> He and his teammates won back-to-back City and State Championships in 1996 and 1997.<ref name="CrenshawAlumni">{{cite web |title=Akbar Gbaja-Biamila – Football and Television Personality |url=http://www.crenshawalumniassoc.org/akbar-gbaja-biamila-football-and-television-personality/ |publisher=Crenshaw High School Alumni Association |access-date=July 26, 2020 |archive-date=July 26, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20200726061317/http://www.crenshawalumniassoc.org/akbar-gbaja-biamila-football-and-television-personality/ |url-status=dead }}</ref> Gbajabiamila moved to play football during his senior year. He was an all-league and all-conference choice. He was also named the team's defensive lineman of the year, compiling 11 sacks and 74 tackles in his senior campaign.<ref name="CrenshawAlumni" />

==College career==
In his senior year, Gbajabiamila received scholarship offers from [[University of Oregon]], [[University of California, Berkeley]], [[San Diego State]], [[Fresno State]], and [[Colorado State]]. He chose to go to [[San Diego State University]], where his older brother also attended.<ref name="USANetwork" /> Gbajabiamila was an all-Mountain West Conference in 2002. He joined the group Athletes For Education, an outreach group that sent players into communities to work with young people on developing their life skills.<ref name="CrenshawAlumni" /> He graduated with a degree in communication and new media studies, before completing a certified entrepreneurship program at the [[Wharton School of Business]] in 2005.<ref name="USANetwork" />

===Oakland Raiders===
Gbajabiamila went undrafted in the [[2003 NFL draft]] and later signed with the [[Oakland Raiders]] as a [[free agent]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Newby |first1=John |title=Akbar Gbaja-Biamila tours Las Vegas Stadium |url=https://247sports.com/nfl/oakland-raiders/Article/Raiders-Las-Vegas-Stadium-tour-Akbar-Gbaja-Biamila-133241096/ |website=247sports.com |date=June 27, 2019}}{{dead link|date=April 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}}</ref> He made the team out of training camp and played in 13 of the team's 16 regular season games.<ref name="CrenshawAlumni" /> He recorded seven tackles (four solos) on the season,<ref name="Pro-Football-Ref">{{cite web |title=Akbar Gbaja-Biamila Stats |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GbajAk20.htm |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com}}</ref> with his first and only sack of the season coming against [[Daunte Culpepper]], then with the [[Minnesota Vikings]].

In 2004, Gbajabiamila split time between defensive end and [[linebacker]], occasionally filling in for players such as [[Travian Smith]] and [[Tyler Brayton]]. He appeared in 14 games for the Raiders during the regular season and was inactive for two games. He accumulated a career-high 14 tackles (11 solo) and added a sack on the year.<ref name="Pro-Football-Ref" /> That sack came against [[Brad Johnson (American football)|Brad Johnson]] and the [[Tampa Bay Buccaneers]], while he recorded a season-high three tackles in games against the [[Denver Broncos]] and [[Jacksonville Jaguars]]. Gbajabiamila also recovered a blocked punt against the [[Carolina Panthers]]  which led to a Raiders touchdown.

Battling injuries during the 2005 training camp, Gbajabiamila was released by the Raiders on September 3. He had a workout with the [[Green Bay Packers]] two days later, but he was not signed and spent the season out of football.

===San Diego Chargers===
Gbajabiamila returned to the NFL in 2006 after being signed by the [[San Diego Chargers]] on January 12. His skills and size was a fit for the 3-4 defense employed by then-defensive coordinator [[Wade Phillips]] and the Chargers.

===Miami Dolphins===
On February 6, 2007, it was announced that Gbajabiamila had been signed to a future contract worth $7.4 million with the Miami Dolphins. The move reunited him with new Dolphins head coach [[Cam Cameron]], who was the offensive coordinator in San Diego the season before when Gbaja-Biamila was a member of the Chargers. On September 11, 2007, he was released by the Dolphins after appearing in one game.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Akbar Gbaja-Biamila 2007 Game Log |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/players/G/GbajAk20/gamelog/2007/ |access-date=2025-02-02 |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en}}</ref> He spent the season out of football.

===Oakland Raiders (second stint)===
Gbajabiamila briefly returned to the Raiders in 2008, but did not appear in a game and was released before the start of the season.

===Other===
In 2005, Gbajabiamila was selected as one of the NFL's first athletes into their Broadcast Boot Camp, held in Mount Laurel, N.J., and designed to give 20 players a short and rigorous look into the skills needed to embark on a broadcast or journalism career after their playing careers. He also took advantage of some time between playing stints to volunteer at KSWB, the NBC affiliate in San Diego, and ended up as the co-host for ''Football Night in San Diego''. He hosted the show for two and a half seasons (2006–2008) before getting one last shot in the NFL with the [[Miami Dolphins]].<ref name="NBC">{{cite web |title=Akbar Gbaja-Biamila Host Bio |url=https://www.nbc.com/american-ninja-warrior/credits/host/akbar-gbaja-Biamila |publisher=NBC |access-date=29 June 2018}}</ref>

==Television career==

With his playing career over, Gbajabiamila turned his focus to the broadcast booth in addition to his philanthropic work, serving as an analyst for the Mtn. Network and CBS Sports Network for two years, while also taking voice and acting classes. He also founded Rush The Passer, a year-round athletic, academic, and life skills program for youth in Southern California.

In 2010 he was approached by reality producer Mark Burnett to be part of a three-man athlete team for his latest project on ABC, ''[[Expedition Impossible (TV series)|Expedition Impossible]]''.<ref name="USANetwork" /> His team "The Football Players" finished in 4th place on the show. That role, and the exposure that came with it, helped further Akbar's exposure.

{{as of|2012}}, he has joined the [[NFL Network]] as a member of the ''NFL Fantasy Live'' cast of hosts. In 2013, he became a color commentator alongside [[Matt Iseman]] for ''[[American Ninja Warrior]]'' being broadcast on [[G4 (U.S. TV channel)|G4]], [[Esquire Network]], and [[NBC]].<ref>{{cite web |last1=Goldberg |first1=Lesley |title='American Ninja Warrior' Adds Pair of New Co-Hosts |url=https://www.hollywoodreporter.com/live-feed/american-ninja-warrior-adds-pair-434771 |publisher=The Hollywood Reporter |date=April 8, 2013}}</ref> The pair also co-hosts ''[[Team Ninja Warrior]]'', a spin-off of ''American Ninja Warrior'' that debuted on Esquire Network in 2016, and ''[[American Ninja Warrior Junior]]'' together on [[Universal Kids]] in 2018.<ref name="NBC" /> The duo provide their voices as themselves in ''[[American Ninja Warrior: Challenge]]''.<ref>{{Cite web|date=2019-01-25|title=American Ninja Warrior Makes The Leap To Video Games, Lands On Switch This March|url=https://www.nintendolife.com/news/2019/01/american_ninja_warrior_makes_the_leap_to_video_games_lands_on_switch_this_march|access-date=2020-11-09|website=Nintendo Life|language=en-GB}}</ref>

On May 10, 2018, Gbajabiamila threw out the first pitch at [[Citizens Bank Park]] before a game between the [[San Francisco Giants]] and [[Philadelphia Phillies]]. The pitch was heavily criticized.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Lott |first1=Thomas |title=Akbar Gbaja-Biamila delivers terrible first pitch |url=https://www.sportingnews.com/ca/mlb/news/mlb-phillies-watch-akbar-gbaja-Biamila-first-pitch-video-worst-ever-raiders/kcmr9yfehj2910j8z7iygjeb7 |publisher=Sporting News |date=May 10, 2018 }}{{Dead link|date=October 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot }}</ref><ref>{{cite web |last1=Pereles |first1=Zach |title=50 Cent may have a challenger for worst first pitch of all time |url=https://sports.yahoo.com/50-cent-may-challenger-worst-first-pitch-time-2-034617863.html |publisher=Yahoo! Sports |date=May 10, 2018}}</ref>

On September 2, 2021, it was announced that Akbar Gbajabiamila would join ''[[The Talk (talk show)|The Talk]]'' as a permanent co-host, and the second full-time male co-host on the show. Gbajabiamila appeared as a guest co-host on multiple episodes in June and July.

In 2024 Gbajabiamila co-hosted the "Stanley Pup," a special produced to air alongside the [[Stanley Cup playoffs]]. The program promoted pet adoption while showing 16 puppies with each dog representing one of the NHL [[2024 Stanley Cup playoffs|2024 playoff]] teams. <ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.nhl.com/news/stanley-pup-show-pairs-hockey-and-animal-rescue| title='Stanley Pup' competition to raise awareness of animal adoption |author= Greenspan, Dan |date=June 4, 2024 |access-date=June 2, 2025|website=NHL.com}}</ref>

==Personal life==

His wife is Chrystal Gbajabiamila.<ref>{{cite web |last1=Ford |first1=Tom |title=Chrystal Gbaja-Biamila Net Worth, Age, Bio, Family & Career |url=https://www.networthy.net/celebrity/chrystal-gbaja-biamila|website=NetWorthy.net |date=November 11, 2023 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20231114140419/https://www.networthy.net/celebrity/chrystal-gbaja-biamila/ |archive-date=November 14, 2023 |url-status=dead}}</ref> His ancestry is [[Nigerian]] of [[Yoruba people|Yoruba]] ethnicity. Both of his parents were [[Muslim]], until his mother converted to [[Christianity]]. He was raised in a [[Sunni]] Muslim household but converted to Christianity while in college.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://blog.chargers.com/2006/07/akbar_gbaja-Biamila_keeps_the_f.html|title=Akbar Gbajabiamila Keeps the Faith|last=Hamilton|first=P. Fox Foundation]], which raises millions of dollars for [[Parkinson's]] research.<ref>{{cite web |title=Akbar Gbajabiamila |url=https://www.michaeljfox.org/bio/akbar-gbaja-Biamila |publisher=Michael J. '''Ahmad Raheem Carroll''' (born August 4, 1983) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] player who was a [[cornerback]] in the [[National Football League]] (NFL). He played [[college football]] for the [[Arkansas Razorbacks football|Arkansas Razorbacks]] and was selected by the [[Green Bay Packers]] in the first round of the [[2004 NFL draft]].

Carroll was also a member of the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]], [[Orlando Predators]], [[New York Jets]], [[Calgary Stampeders]], [[Hartford Colonials]], [[Virginia Destroyers]], [[Arizona Rattlers]] and [[Toronto Argonauts]].

==Early life==
{{BLP unreferenced section|date=May 2025}}
Ahmad Carroll was born August 4, 1983, to Artie and Carrolyn Carroll in [[Atlanta]], Georgia. In his earlier years, Ahmad ran track for the D.C. Motion Track Club and also played Pop Warner football. During his years playing Pop Warner football, he earned the nickname "Batman" after repeatedly jumping over an offensive lineman. He later attended [[Douglass High School (Georgia)|Frederick Douglass High School]] in Atlanta where he was an All-Area cornerback, as well as tailback. Tom Lemming's Prep Football Report rated Ahmad as the nation's No. 26 overall player, while Super Prep rated him as the second-best among all the nation's defensive backs. He was rated the best defensive back in the nation by Prep Star, while Rivals100.com called him the second-best cornerback in the nation. Blue Chip Illustrated rated Ahmad the second-best cornerback in the nation and the fourth-best overall player in Georgia. He was an ESPN/Reebok All-American selection as he recorded 70 tackles as a senior. He chose to accept a scholarship to the [[University of Arkansas]].

==College career==
{{BLP unreferenced section|date=July 2023}}
Carroll excelled in two sports at the [[University of Arkansas]] as both a [[Sprint (running)|sprinter]] for the [[Track and field|track]] team and a cornerback for the football team. He finished his college football career with the following statistics:

*140 [[Tackle (football move)|tackle]]s (7 for losses)
*25 [[pass deflected|passes defensed]]
*4 [[interception]]s
*2 [[fumble]] recoveries
*2 forced fumbles
*12 [[quarterback]] [[Rush (gridiron football)|hurries]]

==Track==
{{BLP unreferenced section|date=July 2023}}

===High school===
While at Frederick Douglass High School, Carroll ran [[track & field]] for the D.C. Motion Track Club. He set a state record in the 100m dash (10.41 seconds) and finished second in the 200-meter dash (21.24 seconds). He was also the national AAU champion in the 100m dash (10.38 seconds) and was selected to Georgia's Magnificent Seven list.

===College===
As an [[University of Arkansas|Arkansas]] collegiate, he competed on the Razorbacks' track team for two seasons. He earned a pair
of All-American honors in the 100m and 200 meters at the 2003 NCAA Outdoor Track and Field Championships.

====2002====
In 2002, during the indoor season, Carroll competed in the [[60 meters|60-meter dash]] and set a new [[University of Arkansas|UA]] record with a provisional qualifying time of 6.69 seconds to win the event at the OU Sooner Invitational. He finished 11th (6.77s) at the SEC Indoor Championships. He also competed in the [[100 meters|100-meter dash]] during the outdoor season. He earned a provisional qualifying time of 10.34 seconds at the SEC Quad and finished third. At the SEC Outdoor Championships, Carroll ran a time of 10.50 seconds in the prelims and just missed advancing to the finals.

====2003====
In 2003, Carroll competed in the [[60 meters|60-meter dash]] during the indoor season. At the Tyson Invitational, he broke his own school record with a time of 6.67 seconds. He finished eighth in the event at the SEC Championships. At the NCAA Championships, he ran a time of 6.73 in the prelims, but was unable to advance to the finals. He ran in the [[100 meters|100]] and [[200 meters|200-meter]] dashes during the outdoor season. He came in fourth (10.34s) in the 100 and third (20.94s) in the 200-meter dash at the SEC Championships. At the NCAA Mideast Regional Championships he registered a career-best time of 10.28 seconds in the prelims of the 100m and in the finals he crossed the line in seventh (10.33s). He went on to finish third (20.89s) in the 200-meter dash to earn an automatic berth to the NCAA Championships. He competed in a total of six races in four days at the NCAA Championships and became the first football letterman since [[Clyde Scott]] in 1948 to score points in an NCAA outdoor meet. He posted a seventh-place finish (10.46s) in the 100m and was the first Razorback athlete to score points in the 100-meter dash and only the second Razorback athlete to earn All-America honors in the event. He earned his second All-America honor for the weekend when he finished eighth in the 200-meter dash with a time of 21.48 seconds. He was the first Arkansas athlete to earn the honor in both the 100m and 200-meter dashes and was the only sprinter for the week to score points in both events.

===Green Bay Packers===
Carroll was drafted by the Green Bay Packers in the first round (25th overall) of the 2004 NFL Draft.<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref> He was the target by many quarterbacks due to his tendency toward illegal contact penalties.  Penalties finally got the best of him when in Week 4 of the [[2006 NFL season|2006 season]] against the [[Philadelphia Eagles]], Carroll was burned for two costly touchdowns by [[Greg Lewis (wide receiver)|Greg Lewis]] and had three penalties. He was cut soon after.

===Jacksonville Jaguars===
In October 2006, Carroll was signed by the [[Jacksonville Jaguars]]. He was waived by the Jaguars on May 7, 2007, following an arrest.

===Orlando Predators===
Carroll played for the [[Orlando Predators]] of the [[Arena Football League (1987–2008)|Arena Football League]] in 2008.

===New York Jets===
Following the 2008 AFL season, Carroll was signed by the [[New York Jets]]. He tried out for the team in 2007 but did not sign a contract.<ref>[http://www.nydailynews.com/sports/football/jets/2007/12/29/2007-12-29_bob_sutton_may_be_jets_scapegoat.html Bob Sutton may be Jets' scapegoat]</ref> He was re-signed by the team on March 16, 2009.<ref>[https://news.yahoo.com/s/ap/20090316/ap_on_sp_fo_ne/fbn_jets_carroll;_ylt=AoBAartshWbX.wEPxv0XWD_IyLQF Jets Re-Sign Carroll] Yahoo Sports, March 16, 2009</ref> Carroll was waived by the New York Jets on November 16, 2009.

===Toronto Argonauts===
On May 10, 2012, Carroll was signed by the [[Toronto Argonauts]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=http://tsn.ca/cfl/story/?id=395566 |title=Argos Sign Four Imports Including Former NFL CB Carroll |access-date=May 13, 2012 |archive-date=May 13, 2012 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120513090102/http://www.tsn.ca/cfl/story/?id=395566 |url-status=dead }}</ref>

On June 30, 2012, Carroll played in his first CFL game against the [[Edmonton Eskimos]].  Midway through the third quarter, Carroll was flagged for defensive pass interference on a deep attempt by Eskimo quarterback [[Steven Jyles]] to receiver [[Fred Stamps]].  The penalty led to an Edmonton field goal, and Toronto went on to lose the game 19–15.

Carroll announced his retirement after winning the Grey Cup in 2012.

|url=https://www.latimes.com/archives/la-xpm-2004-dec-24-sp-nflrep24-story.html |access-date=June 1, 2018 |website=[[Los Angeles Times]]}} The Arizona Cardinals' new head coach [[Dennis Green]] retained Wilson as the starting strong safety to start the regular season, along with free safety [[Quentin Harris (American football)|Quentin Harris]].{{Cite web |title=The Football Database: Arizona Cardinals Roster (2004) |url=https://www.footballdb.com/teams/nfl/arizona-cardinals/roster/2004 |access-date=June 2, 2018 |website=footballdb.com}} On September 19, 2004, Wilson recorded a season-high 11 combined tackles (ten solo) and two pass deflections during a 23–12 loss to the [[2004 New England Patriots|New England Patriots]].{{Cite web |title=NFL Player stats: Adrian Wilson (2004) |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/adrianwilson/2504754/gamelogs?season=2004 |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=NFL.com}} Wilson completed the [[2004 NFL season|2004 season]] with 102 combined tackles (80 solo), eight pass deflections, three interceptions, and a sack in 16 games and 16 starts. ====2005==== Defensive coordinator [[Clancy Pendergast]] chose to retain Wilson as the starting strong safety to start the 2005 regular season, opposite free safety [[Robert Griffith]].{{Cite web |title=The Football Database: Arizona Cardinals Roster (2005) |url=https://www.footballdb.com/teams/nfl/arizona-cardinals/roster/2005 |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=footballdb.com}}{{Cite web |date=June 7, 2018 |title=Pro-Football-Reference: 2005 Arizona Cardinals (Starters/Roster) |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/teams/crd/2005_roster.htm |website=[[Pro Football Reference]]}} In Week 3, Wilson collected 11 combined tackles (six solo) and a pass deflection in the Cardinals' 37–12 loss at the [[2005 Seattle Seahawks|Seattle Seahawks]]. On November 13, 2005, he collected a season-high 14 combined tackles (ten solo) and two pass deflections in a 29–21 loss at the [[2005 Detroit Lions|Detroit Lions]] in Week 10. The following week, Wilson made eight solo tackles and a career-high three sacks on quarterback [[Marc Bulger]] during a 38–28 victory at the [[2005 St. Louis Rams|St. Louis Rams]] in Week 11.{{Cite web |title=NFL Player stats: Adrian Wilson (2005) |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/adrianwilson/2504754/gamelogs?season=2005 |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=NFL.com}} In Week 16, Wilson recorded five solo tackles, a pass deflection, and made two sacks on quarterback [[Donovan McNabb]] in the Cardinals' 27–21 win against the [[2005 Philadelphia Eagles|Philadelphia Eagles]]. He finished the [[2005 NFL season|2005 season]] with a career-high 109 combined tackles (93 solo), eight passes defensed, a career-high eight sacks, a forced fumble, and an interception in 16 games and 16 starts. ====2006==== Head coach Dennis Green retained Wilson and Robert Smith as the starting safety duo to begin the season in 2006.{{Cite web |title=the Football Database: Arizona Cardinals Roster (2006) |url=https://www.footballdb.com/teams/nfl/arizona-cardinals/roster/2006 |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=footballdb.com}} On October 1, 2006, Wilson recorded five combined tackles, a pass deflection, and returned an interception by quarterback [[Michael Vick]] for a 99-yard touchdown as the Cardinals lost 32–10 at the [[2006 Atlanta Falcons|Atlanta Falcons]].{{Cite web |date=November 24, 2008 |title=Reed rumbles 108 yards for NFL record {{!}} Longest interception returns by team |url=http://www.profootballhof.com/hof/release.aspx?release_id=2959 |access-date=June 2, 2014 |website=[[Pro Football Hall of Fame]]}} In Week 13, he collected a season-high nine solo tackles, broke up two passes, and an interception in a 34–20 victory at the [[2006 St. Louis Rams|St. Louis Rams]].{{Cite web |title=NFL Player stats: Adrian Wilson (2006) |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/adrianwilson/2504754/gamelogs?season=2006 |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=NFL.com}} On December 20, 2006, it was announced that Wilson was selected to play in the [[2007 Pro Bowl]], marking his first career [[Pro Bowl]] selection. He finished the season with a total of 82 combined tackles (74 solo), seven pass deflections, five sacks, four interceptions, and a touchdown in 16 games and 16 starts. ====2007==== On January 1, 2007, the Arizona Cardinals fired head coach Dennis Green after they completed the 2006 season with a 5–11 record.{{Cite web |date=January 1, 2007 |title=Cardinals fire coach Green after three years |url=https://www.washingtonpost.com/wp-dyn/content/article/2007/01/01/AR2007010100316_pf.html |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=washingtonpost.com}} The Arizona Cardinals' new head coach [[Ken Whisenhunt]] retained Wilson as the starting strong safety to start the regular season, alongside free safety [[Terrence Holt]].{{Cite web |title=Ourlads.com: Arizona Cardinals Depth Chart: 09/02/2007 |url=http://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/17/ARZ |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=Ourlads.com}} He started in the [[2007 Arizona Cardinals|Arizona Cardinals']] season-opener at the [[2007 San Francisco 49ers|San Francisco 49ers]] and collected ten combined tackles (six solo) and a pass deflection in their 20–17 loss. On September 23, 2007, Wilson recorded a season-high 12 combined tackles (ten solo) during a 26–23 loss at the [[2007 Baltimore Ravens|Baltimore Ravens]] in Week 3. In Week 5, he made two solo tackles, a pass deflection, and an interception in the Cardinals' 34–31 win at the [[2007 St. Louis Rams|St. Louis Rams]].{{Cite web |title=NFL Player stats: Adrian Wilson (2007) |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/adrianwilson/2504754/gamelogs?season=2007 |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=NFL.com}} The interception marked his second consecutive interception of the season. In Week 10, Wilson sustained an injured to his heel and was inactive for the next two games (Weeks 11–12).{{Cite web |date=November 25, 2007 |title=49ers' Alex Smith, Cardinals' Adrian Wilson sit out game |url=https://www.eastbaytimes.com/2007/11/25/49ers-alex-smith-cardinals-adrian-wilson-sit-out-game/ |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=eastbaytimes.com |agency=Associated Press}} Hie injury ended his 59-game streak of consecutive starts. On November 28, 2007, the Arizona Cardinals placed Wilson on [[injured reserve]] for the remainder of the season after it was confirmed he would have to undergo surgery to repair a torn [[Achilles tendon]] and an injury he sustained to his right heel.{{Cite web |last=Pasquerelli, Len |date=November 28, 2007 |title=Wilson joins fellow DB Green on injured list, out for season |url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3131664 |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=ESPN.com}} Wilson completed his first season under Ken Whisenhunt with a total of 44 combined tackles (33 solo), three pass deflections, and two interceptions in nine games and nine starts. ====2008==== Wilson returned as the starting strong safety in 2008 and was paired with free safety [[Antrel Rolle]]. The Cardinals' secondary also included cornerbacks [[Eric Green (cornerback)|Eric Green]], [[Roderick Hood]], and rookie [[Dominique Rodgers-Cromartie]].{{Cite web |title=Ourlads.com: Arizona Cardinals Depth Chart: 08/29/2008 |url=http://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/29/ARZ |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=ourlads.com}} He started in the [[2008 Arizona Cardinals|Arizona Cardinals']] season-opener at the [[2008 San Francisco 49ers|San Francisco 49ers]] and made four combined tackles, a pass deflection, and intercepted a pass by quarterback [[J. T. O'Sullivan]] in their 23–13 victory.{{Cite web |title=NFL Game Center: Week 1-2008: Arizona Cardinals @ San Francisco 49ers |url=http://www.nfl.com/gamecenter/2008090711/2008/REG1/cardinals@49ers |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=NFL.com}} Wilson was inactive for the Cardinals' Week 4 loss at the [[2008 New York Jets|New York Jets]]. On October 8, 2008, Wilson received a $25,000 fine for roughing the passer. The fine was from a Week 5 incident where he drove quarterback [[Trent Edwards]] into the ground. Edwards was immediately rendered unconscious from the hit and caused a concussion.{{Cite web |title=Adrian Wilson fined $25,000 for Trent Edwards hit |url=https://www.profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2008/10/10/adrian-wilson-fined-25000-for-trent-edwards-hit/ |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20170115073622/http://profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/2008/10/10/adrian-wilson-fined-25000-for-trent-edwards-hit/ |archive-date=January 15, 2017 |access-date=June 3, 2018 |website=profootballtalk.nbcsports.com/}} On November 23, 2008, Wilson collected a season-high nine combined tackles (seven solo) during a 37–29 loss to the [[2008 New York Giants|New York Giants]] in Week 13. On December 17, 2008, it was announced that Wilson was selected to play in the [[2009 Pro Bowl]].{{Cite web |title=2009 Pro Bowl Rosters |url=http://zimbio.com/AFC-NFC+Pro+Bowl/articles/2/2009+Pro+Bowl+Roster+Announced |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=zimbio.com}} Wilson finished the [[2008 NFL season|2008 season]] with 75 combined tackles (60 solo), five pass deflections, 2.5 sacks, and two interceptions in 15 games and 15 starts. The Arizona Cardinals finished the season first in the [[NFC West]] with a 9–7 record. On January 3, 2009, Wilson started his first career playoff game and recorded four solo tackles in a 30–24 victory against the [[2008 Atlanta Falcons|Atlanta Falcons]] in the NFC Wildcard Game. The Cardinals defeating the [[2008 Carolina Panthers|Carolina Panthers]] 33–13 in the NFC Divisional Round. On January 18, 2009, Wilson collected seven solo tackles, deflected a pass, and made two sacks in a 32–25 victory at the [[2008 Philadelphia Eagles|Philadelphia Eagles]] in the [[NFC Championship Game]]. On February 1, 2009, Wilson recorded seven solo tackles in the Cardinals' 27–23 loss to the [[2008 Pittsburgh Steelers|Pittsburgh Steelers]] in [[Super Bowl XLIII]].{{Cite web |title=NFL Player stats: Adrian Wilson (2008) |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/adrianwilson/2504754/gamelogs?season=2008 |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=[[NFL.com]]}} ====2009==== On February 9, 2009, head coach Ken Whisenhunt fired defensive coordinator Clancy Pendergast. Pendergast was Wilson's defensive coordinator for the last six seasons.{{Cite web |date=February 9, 2009 |title=Cards oust D-coordinator Pendergast |url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=3891143 |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=ESPN.com}} On June 4, 2009, the Arizona Cardinals re-signed Wilson to a five-year, $39 million contract extension with $18.50 million guaranteed. The contract extension added four additional years to Wilson's previous contract that had one-year remaining.{{Cite web |date=June 5, 2009 |title=Wilson gets new deal from Cardinals |url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=4231534 |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=ESPN.com}} Defensive coordinator [[Billy Davis (American football coach)|Billy Davis]] retained Wilson and Antrel Rolle as the starting safety duo to begin the regular season.{{Cite web |title=Ourlads.com: Arizona Cardinals Depth Chart: 09/06/2009 |url=http://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/40/ARZ |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=Ourlads.com}} On December 14, 2009, Wilson recorded a season-high eight solo tackles, a career-high five pass deflections, and an interception during a 24–9 loss at the [[2009 San Francisco 49ers|San Francisco 49ers]] in Week 14. On December 26, 2009, Wilson recorded four solo tackles, a pass deflection, an interception, and a sack during a 31–19 victory against the [[2009 St. Louis Rams|St. Louis Rams]]. His sack was the 20th of his career and earned him the recognition of being the 14th player to record 20 sacks and 20 interceptions in their career and become the a member of the 20–20 club.{{Cite web |last=Gribble, Andrew |date=October 16, 2015 |title=Karlos Dansby's 2 INTs move him closer to exclusive statistical milestone |url=http://clevelandbrowns.com/news/article-5/Karlos-Dansby’s-2-INTs-move-him-closer-to-exclusive-statistical-milestone/89cbbde5-e59a-4895-918c-5cb3145e49f5 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160520152744/http://www.clevelandbrowns.com/news/article-5/Karlos-Dansby%E2%80%99s-2-INTs-move-him-closer-to-exclusive-statistical-milestone/89cbbde5-e59a-4895-918c-5cb3145e49f5 |archive-date=May 20, 2016 |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=ClevelandBrowns.com}}{{Cite news |last=Young |first=Bob |date=June 4, 2009 |title=Cardinals sign Wilson; shift focus |work=The Arizona Republic |url=https://www.azcentral.com/sports/cardinals/articles/2009/06/04/20090604adrianwilson.html }}{{Dead link|date=August 2025 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} On December 29, 2009, Wilson was voted to the [[2010 Pro Bowl]], marking the third selection of his career.{{Cite web |date=December 30, 2009 |title=2010 AFC & NFC Pro Bowl Rosters |url=https://www.baltimorebeatdown.com/platform/2009/12/30/1227108/2010-afc-nfc-pro-bowl-rosters |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=baltimorebeatdown.com}}{{Dead link|date=September 2019 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }} Wilson completed the [[2009 NFL season|2009 season]] with 74 combined tackles (61 solo), 13 passes defensed, five interceptions, and two sacks in 16 games and 16 starts. The [[2009 Arizona Cardinals|Arizona Cardinals]] finished atop The NFC West with a 10–6 record and clinched a wildcard berth. On January 16, 2010, Wilson recorded nine combined tackles and a pass deflection during a 45–14 loss at the [[2009 New Orleans Saints|New Orleans Saints]] in the NFC Divisional Round.{{Cite web |title=NFL Player stats: Adrian Wilson (2009) |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/adrianwilson/2504754/gamelogs?season=2009 |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=NFL.com}} ====2010==== Head coach Ken Whisenhunt retained Wilson as the starting strong safety in 2010, alongside free safety [[Kerry Rhodes]].{{Cite web |title=Ourlads.com: Arizona Cardinals Depth Chart: 09/05/2010 |url=http://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/111/ARZ |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=Ourlads.com}} He started in the [[2010 Arizona Cardinals|Arizona Cardinals']] season-opener at the [[2010 St. Louis Rams|St. Louis Rams]] and recorded two solo tackles, two pass deflections, a sack, and intercepted two passes by quarterback [[Sam Bradford]] in their 17–13 victory. In Week 14, he collected a season-high 11 solo tackles and a pass deflection during a 43–13 victory against the [[2010 Denver Broncos|Denver Broncos]]. He completed the season with 88 combined tackles (76 solo), nine pass deflections, two interceptions, and two sacks in 16 games and 16 starts. He was ranked 89th by his fellow players on the [[NFL Top 100 Players of 2011]].{{Cite web |title=2011 NFL Top 100 |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/awards/2011-nfl-top-100.htm |access-date=2024-03-18 |website=[[Pro Football Reference]] |language=en}} ====2011==== On January 6, 2011, Arizona Cardinals' head coach [[Ken Whisenhunt]] fired defensive coordinator Bill Davis after the team finished with a 5–11 record in 2010.{{Cite web |date=January 6, 2011 |title=Cardinals fire coordinator Bill Davis |url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/news/story?id=5996811 |access-date=June 5, 2018 |website=ESPN.com |agency=Associated Press}} Their new defensive coordinator, [[Ray Horton]], retained both Wilson and Kerry Rhodes as the starting safety tandem to begin the regular season. On December 18, 2011, Wilson collected a season-high eight solo tackles and deflected a pass during a 20–17 victory against the [[2011 Cleveland Browns|Cleveland Browns]] in Week 15.{{Cite web |title=NFL Player stats: Adrian Wilson (2011) |url=http://www.nfl.com/player/adrianwilson/2504754/gamelogs?season=2011 |access-date=June 5, 2018 |website=NFL.com}} On December 27, 2011, Wilson was selected to play in the [[2012 Pro Bowl]], marking his fourth Pro Bowl appearance of his career.{{Cite web |date=December 27, 2011 |title=2012 Pro Bowl Rosters |url=http://www.nfl.com/probowl/story/09000d5d82578253/article/2012-pro-bowl-rosters |access-date=June 5, 2011 |website=NFL.com}} He finished the 2012 season with 65 combined tackles (48 solo), 14 passes defensed, and an interception in 16 games and 16 starts. ====2012==== On July 25, 2012, Wilson agreed to restructure his contract to help the Cardinals free up additional cap space.{{Cite web |last=Breed, Albert |date=June 24, 2012 |title=Adrian Wilson signs Arizona Cardinals contract extension through 2015 |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/adrian-wilson-signs-arizona-cardinals-contract-extension-throug-09000d5d82ac6b96 |access-date=June 4, 2018 |website=NFL.com}} Head coach Ken Whisenhunt retained Wilson and Rhodes as the starting safety duo in 2012. In a Week 1 win against the division rival [[2012 Seattle Seahawks season|Seattle Seahawks]] Wilson intercepted rookie quarterback [[Russell Wilson]], this was the first interception in Russell Wilson's career. Wilson was inactive for the Cardinals' Week 3 victory against the [[2012 Philadelphia Eagles|Philadelphia Eagles]] after injuring his groin and ankle. The injuries ended his streak of 62 consecutive regular season games played.{{Cite web |last=McIntyre, Brian |date=September 23, 2012 |title=Adrian Wilson, Knowshon Moreno headline late game NFL inactive lists |url=https://www.yahoo.com/amphtml/blogs/shutdown-corner/adrian-wilson-knowshon-moreno-headline-game-nfl-inactive-190625831--nfl.html |access-date=June 5, 2018 |website=Yahoo.com}} In Week 4, he collected a season-high ten combined tackles (eight solo), three pass deflections, a forced fumble, and sacked quarterback [[Ryan Tannehill]] during a 24–21 overtime victory against the [[2012 Miami Dolphins|Miami Dolphins]].{{Cite web |title=NFL Game Center: Week 4-2012: Miami Dolphins @ Arizona Cardinals |url=http://www.nfl.com/gamecenter/2012093007/2012/REG4/dolphins@cardinals |access-date=June 5, 2018 |website=NFL.com}} On December 16, 2012, Wilson recorded three solo tackles and sacked quarterback [[Matthew Stafford]] during a 38–10 win against the [[2012 Detroit Lions|Detroit Lions]] in Week 15. The sack brought his career total to 25 sacks. Along with his 27 interceptions, Wilson became only the sixth player in league history to earn 25 sacks and 25 interceptions over the course of their career and join the vaunted 25–25 club.{{Cite news |last=Young |first=Bob |date=December 16, 2012 |title=Adrian Wilson affirms stamp on Arizona Cardinals history |work=The Arizona Republic |url=https://www.azcentral.com/sports/cardinals/articles/20121216adrian-wilson-affirms-stamp-arizona-cardinals-history.html |archive-date=December 21, 2012 |access-date=April 16, 2020 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121221011203/http://www.azcentral.com/sports/cardinals/articles/20121216adrian-wilson-affirms-stamp-arizona-cardinals-history.html |url-status=dead }} He completed his last season with the Cardinals with a total of 54 combined tackles (39 solo), five pass deflections, three sacks, a forced fumble, and an interception in 15 games and 14 starts. ====2013==== On January 3, 2013, the Arizona Cardinals fired general manager [[Rod Graves]] and head coach Ken Whisenhunt after they did not qualify for the playoffs after finishing with a 5–11 record in 2012.{{Cite web |date=December 31, 2012 |title=Cards fire Ken Whisenhunt, Graves |url=http://www.espn.com/nfl/story/_/id/8796471/arizona-cardinals-fire-ken-whisenhunt-rod-graves |access-date=June 5, 2018 |website=ESPN.com}} On March 8, 2013, the Arizona Cardinals released Wilson ending his 12-year tenure with the team. ====New England Patriots==== On March 15, 2013, the [[New England Patriots]] signed Wilson to a three-year, $5 million contract that includes a signing bonus of $1 million.{{Cite web |last=Young, Shaleese |date=March 19, 2013 |title=Contract details for Aqib Talib and Adrian Wilson |url=https://www.boston.com/sports/new-england-patriots/2013/03/19/contract_detail-2/ |access-date=June 5, 2018 |website=Boston.com}} Upon joining the team, Wilson offered [[Kyle Arrington]] a year's supply of diapers for Arrington's newborn baby to have his jersey No. 24, the number Wilson had in Arizona. On May 1, 2013, Wilson received the No. 24 jersey from Kyle Arrington. Kyle Arrington was reassigned to No. 25.[http://espn.go.com/blog/boston/new-englandpatriots/post/_/id/4741094/adrian-wilson-pats-reach-agreement]{{dead link|date=July 2024|bot=medic}}{{cbignore|bot=medic}} During training camp, Wilson competed to be the starting strong safety against [[Duron Harmon]] and [[Steve Gregory (American football)|Steve Gregory]].{{Cite web |title=Ourlads.com: New England Patriots Depth Chart: 07/01/2013 |url=http://www.ourlads.com/nfldepthcharts/archive/146/NE |access-date=June 5, 2018 |website=Ourlads.com}} On August 31, 2013, the New England Patriots placed Wilson on the season-ending injured reserve due to an Achilles tendon injury. On April 4, 2014, the New England Patriots released Wilson.{{Cite web |title=Adrian Wilson released by New England Patriots |url=https://www.nfl.com/news/adrian-wilson-released-by-new-england-patriots-0ap2000000339501 |access-date=November 10, 2021 |website=NFL.com}} ====Chicago Bears==== On June 23, 2014, the [[Chicago Bears]] signed Wilson to a one-year, $955,000 contract at the veteran minimum. Throughout training camp, he competed against [[Ryan Mundy]] for the job as the starting strong safety. '''Adrien Carlton Clarke''' (born March 26, 1981) is an American former professional [[American football|football]] [[Guard (American football)|guard]]. He was selected by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in the seventh round of the [[2004 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] at [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State]].

Clarke was also a member of the [[New York Jets]], [[Baltimore Ravens]], [[Florida Tuskers]], and [[Virginia Destroyers]].

==College career==
Clarke played [[college football]] for the [[Ohio State Buckeyes football|Ohio State Buckeyes]] and started in 43 games in his career.<ref name="Draft">{{cite news |title=Buckeyes break record with 14 players chosen |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=xWpcAAAAIBAJ&sjid=klcNAAAAIBAJ&pg=1532,7398773 |newspaper=[[The Vindicator]] |date=April 26, 2004 |access-date=2010-10-28}}</ref> Following the 2003 season, he was invited to play in the 2004 [[Senior Bowl]].<ref>{{cite news |title=BG's Harris on North in Senior Bowl |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=K11IAAAAIBAJ&sjid=NgQEAAAAIBAJ&pg=1432,2279543 |newspaper=[[Toledo Blade]] |date=January 24, 2004 |access-date=2010-10-28}}</ref> He also won the 2002 national championship against [[Miami Hurricanes football|Miami]].

==Professional career==

===Philadelphia Eagles===
Clarke was selected by the [[Philadelphia Eagles]] in the seventh round (227th overall) of the [[2004 NFL draft]].<ref>{{Cite web |url=https://www.pro-football-reference.com/years/2004/draft.htm |title=2004 NFL Draft Listing |website=Pro-Football-Reference.com |language=en |access-date=2023-05-06}}</ref> He was signed to a four-year contract on July 15, 2004.<ref>{{cite news |title=TRANSACTIONS |url=https://select.nytimes.com/gst/abstract.html?res=F40D16F63C5E0C768DDDAE0894DC404482 |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=July 15, 2004 |access-date=2010-10-28}}</ref> He was placed on the [[injured reserve list]] at the beginning of the [[2004 NFL season|2004 season]] after suffering a torn hamstring.<ref>{{cite news |author=Patton, Steve |title=Birds will face Giants at nearly full strength |url=https://news.google.com/newspapers?id=oPghAAAAIBAJ&sjid=iaIFAAAAIBAJ&pg=1329,5272163 |newspaper=[[Reading Eagle]] |date=September 9, 2004 |access-date=2010-10-28}}</ref>

Clarke made his first NFL start in week 12 of the [[2005 NFL season|2005 season]], replacing injured left guard [[Artis Hicks]].<ref>{{cite news |title=Next For Seahawks: Philadelphia Eagles |url=http://www.seattlepi.com/football/250238_hnext30.html |work=[[Seattle Post-Intelligencer]] |date=November 30, 2005 |access-date=2010-10-28}}</ref> He started in four games total in 2005.<ref>{{cite news|title=Fraley hoping versatility pays off |url=http://www.pittsburghlive.com/x/pittsburghtrib/news/today/s_467557.html |work=[[Pittsburgh Tribune-Review]] |date=August 24, 2006 |access-date=2010-10-28 }}{{dead link|date=June 2017 |bot=InternetArchiveBot |fix-attempted=yes }}</ref>

Clarke was waived/injured on August 29, 2006, due to a back injury that required surgery.<ref>{{cite news|title=Eagles Place Bloom On Injured Reserve List |url=http://www.wsbtv.com/sports/9757699/detail.html |work=wsbtv.com |date=August 29, 2006 |access-date=2010-10-28 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110629135452/http://www.wsbtv.com/sports/9757699/detail.html |archive-date=2011-06-29 }}</ref><ref name="Jets">{{cite news |author=Crouse, Karen |title=Jets' O-Line Must Be Great for Offense to Be Good |url=http://fifthdown.blogs.nytimes.com/2007/09/14/jets-o-line-must-be-great-for-offense-to-be-good/ |work=[[The New York Times]] |date=September 14, 2007 |access-date=2010-10-28}}</ref>

===New York Jets===
Clarke was signed by the [[New York Jets]] to a reserve/future contract on January 22, 2007.<ref>{{cite news |author=Roberts, Lee |title=Jets sign guard Adrien Clarke |url=http://nyj.scout.com/2/611975.html?refid=400&cmp=otc-k9b140813162&att=5 |work=[[scout.com]] |date=January 22, 2007 |access-date=2010-10-28 |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110716021452/http://nyj.scout.com/2/611975.html?refid=400&cmp=otc-k9b140813162&att=5 |archive-date=2011-07-16 |url-status=dead }}</ref> Clarke earned the starting left guard job in the preseason<ref name="Jets"/> and started in 14 games in [[2007 NFL season|2007]].<ref name="Waived">{{cite news |title=Jets cut ties with Dyson, McCareins, Clarke |url=http://www.seattlepi.com/scorecard/nflnews.asp?articleID=162876 |work=[[Seattle Post-Intelligencer]] |date=February 26, 2008 |access-date=2010-10-29 }} {{Dead link|date=December 2011|bot=RjwilmsiBot}}</ref>

He was waived on February 26, 2008.<ref name="Waived"/>

===Baltimore Ravens===
On May 16, 2008, Clarke was signed by the [[Baltimore Ravens]], but was released on August 30.<ref>{{cite news|title=Stills among Ravens' cuts |url=http://www.fredericknewspost.com/sections/sports/display.htm?StoryID=79533 |work=[[Frederick News-Post]] |date=August 31, 2008 |access-date=2010-10-29 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120328175029/http://www.fredericknewspost.com/sections/sports/display.htm?StoryID=79533 |archive-date=2012-03-28 }}</ref>

===Florida Tuskers===
Clarke was drafted by the [[Florida Tuskers]] of the [[United Football League (2009–)|United Football League]] in the sixth round (29th overall) of the [[2010 UFL draft]]. He started the 2010 season at right guard and was resigned in 2011 and will go into camp as the incumbent right guard for the now [[Virginia Destroyers]].

'''Airese K. Currie''' (born November 16, 1982) is an American former professional [[Gridiron football|football]] [[wide receiver]]. He was selected by the [[Chicago Bears]] in the fifth round of the [[2005 NFL draft]]. He played [[college football]] for the [[Clemson Tigers football|Clemson Tigers]].

Currie was also a member of the [[BC Lions]] and [[Hamilton Tiger-Cats]].

==Early life==
Currie attended [[Richland Northeast High School]] in [[Columbia, South Carolina]], and was a [[Letterman (sports)|letterman]] in [[High school football|football]] and [[Track and field|track]]. In track, he was the South Carolina state champion on the [[200 m|200]] and the [[400 m]]eter dashes, and ran a personal best of 10.22 seconds on the [[100 m]]eter dash.

==College career==
Currie attended [[Clemson University]] and was a letterman in [[College football|football]] and track. In track, he was a three-time All-[[Atlantic Coast Conference]] selection, and as a senior, he won the [[NCAA]] Regional East title on the 100 meter dash.

===Track and field===
Currie was also a track star. He was a three-time All-[[Atlantic Coast Conference]] selection, and as a senior, he won the [[NCAA]] Regional East title on the 100 meter dash, posting a time of 10.22 seconds.

In 2004, he ran anchor for the Tigers' [[4 × 100 meter relay]] team, which was ranked as the 14th-fastest time of that season. He also ran the [[60 meters]] and [[200 meters]], posting personal bests of 6.79 seconds and 20.65 seconds, respectively.

'''Aki Jones''' (October 25, 1982 – October 12, 2014) was an American [[American football|football]] player, who played in [[National Football League]] for [[Washington Redskins]] in [[2005 NFL season|2005 season]]. He signed a 3-year contract to the Washington Redskins as an Undrafted Free Agent at the end of the [[2005 NFL draft]].

He also played professionally in Europe for several teams, but played in Poland [[Polish American Football Association]] and Finland [[Vaahteraliiga]] for much of his European career.

Jones played a cameo role in a 2011 Polish comedy ''Wojna żeńsko-męska'' (''The Female-Male War'').

Aki Jones died in car accident in [[Miami]].<ref>{{cite web | title = Nie żyje Aki Jones. Były futbolista The Crew zginął w wypadku | language = Polish | publisher = mmwroclaw.pl | date = 13 Oct 2014 | url = http://www.mmwroclaw.pl/494559/nie-zyje-aki-jones-byly-futbolista-the-crew-zginal-w-wypadku | accessdate = 13 Oct 2014 }}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.touchdown-europe.net/2014/10/in-memoriam-aki-jones-1982-2014.html|title = In Memoriam: Aki Jones (1982-2014)}}</ref><ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.americanfootballinternational.com/aki-jones-1982-2014/|title = Remembering Aki Jones: 1982 - 2014|date = 13 October 2015}}</ref>

==High school==
===Christ the King Regional High School===
Born in [[Jamaica, New York|Jamaica]], [[New York (state)|New York]], Jones initially attended St. John's Prep High School in Queens, NY in 2000. While at St. John's he played only basketball due to them not having a football team. in 2001, his Sophomore year, he transferred to Christ the King Regional H.S in Middle Village, Queens so that he could have the opportunity to play football. His senior year, he received All-City and All League Honors. Jones was selected to play in CHSFL (Catholic High School Football League) All-Star game and represented New York City in the annual NYC vs Long Island [http://www.empirechallenge.com/ Outback Steakhouse Empire Challenge].

===Deerfield Academy===
Jones attended [[Deerfield Academy]] in Deerfield, Massachusetts for a [[postgraduate year]]. While at Deerfield he played varsity football, basketball and track and field. In his first year of track and field Jones placed 5th in New England's Regional Meet in the discus and shot put.

==College career==
In 2001 Jones attended [[Fordham University]] in the Bronx, New York. Jones contribute on both O Line and D Line his freshman year. Jones was a starter his junior and senior year. In 2003 Jones received First-team All-Patriot League Honors. During his senior year, he received Lindy's Pre-Season 1-AA Second-team All-American and Second-team All-Patriot League Honors. Jones finished his career at Fordham with a 2002 Patriot League Championship and team leader in sacks for three consecutive years 2002, 2003, and 2004. He graduated from the [[Gabelli School of Business]] in 2009.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://fordhamsports.com/news/2016/2/2/FB_0202160319.aspx|work=Fordham University Rams|title=Former Football Ram Aki Jones Inducted into AFNT Hall of Fame|date=February 2, 2016|accessdate=May 2, 2017}}</ref>

==NFL==
Jones signed with the Washington Redskins as an undrafted free agent in April 2005. Jones spent the opening day roster on the practice squad but was elevated to active roster by week 2. Jones appeared in his first game on November 6, 2005, against the Philadelphia Eagles where he registered his first tackle. In the [[2005 NFL season]] he played in four games which remains his only season.

==European career==
In March 2007, Jones moved to Poland where he worked as President/Creator of the ''Super Flag Bol'' league in  [[Wrocław]], which is the first junior high school [[flag football]] league in Poland.

Jones was also a player for [[The Crew Wrocław]] an American football club in the [[Polish American Football League]]. He also played for the [[Warsaw Eagles]] in Poland's top league.

In 2011, he moved to Sweden and joined the [[Arlanda Jets]], who play in the Swedish [[Superserien]].

In 2013, he signed with Turku Trojans who play in the [[Vaahteraliiga]] Maple League the top level in Finland.

In 2013, he moved to Brazil and declared to participate in the LFA, which is the Brazilian NFL.

During the summer, he joined the [[Turku Trojans]] for the 2014 season, the Trojans were then playing in the Finnish 1st division, the second highest level league in Finland.

Jones had returned from Europe prior to his death, and had taken a position as a Group Sales Account Executive with the [[Miami Dolphins]].

He died in a car accident in October 2014.
